text: Use ChatGPT to generate a company name for the GMB profile; the name does not affect ranking or conversion so spend no more than 2 minutes on it.

For the GMB profile address, choose a large commercial office building with no storefront presence (multi-tenant tower) to minimize the chance of address-related complaints; avoid residential addresses where someone might notice a business listed there.

When ranking a new GMB profile, prioritize adding fake reviews early (every competitor does it, per speaker) along with keyword-rich descriptions; a separate video covers the full step-by-step ranking process.

When approaching a potential lead-buyer who already runs Google Ads in your service category, frame your offer as cheaper than their current cost-per-call from Google; they will immediately see the math and agree.

To verify that a city-niche combo is worth pursuing, check SEMrush keyword overview for monthly search volume (must be 400+) and then check Google Maps top-3 competitors for review counts and ratings before investing setup time.

Start with a local city or suburb you already know rather than an unfamiliar market; familiarity reduces friction in choosing addresses, finding subcontractors, and understanding local service demand patterns.

When building a brand, curate which pairings to pursue and which to avoid with the same intentionality as a gardener — add good associations and actively remove or avoid bad ones; do not let the brand form by accident through whatever it happens to appear next to.
If charging a premium price, ensure the product is dialed to a high standard so that the post-purchase experience reinforces rather than undermines the brand association built through marketing.

When recovering from a negative brand event (controversial pairing, public mistake, product failure), do not attempt to erase it — instead overwhelm it with a high volume of positive pairings until the negative association shrinks into statistical irrelevance relative to the aggregate.

Measure brand-building efforts against three observable metrics: Influence (does recognition change behavior?), Direction (is the behavior change toward or away from the brand?), and Reach (how many people does it change behavior for?). Use these as the only objective tests of whether brand investment is working.

When evaluating any new brand pairing (new content type, collaboration, product category), treat it as a net-audience bet: accept that some existing audience members will leave, and make the pairing only if you have reason to believe the new audience gained will exceed the existing audience lost.

When someone discloses something material to you, respond at the moment of disclosure with a neutral or positive acknowledgment to reinforce that sharing was safe (e.g., your secret is safe with me; it is your news to share how you choose).

Before breaking your word when a short-term benefit is available, explicitly calculate whether the short-term gain outweighs the long-term cost to the relationship; in most ongoing relationships, it will not.

When evaluating whether to trust someone, identify specific past instances when you made yourself punishable to them and whether they used that against you; use those instances as your evidence base rather than vague feelings.

As a leader, proactively share context and information with your team that they could theoretically use against you; this extends default trust and raises the stakes for team members to behave consistently with that trust.
When evaluating whether to work at a job, ask whether the work is earning (paycheck is material) or learning (knowledge is material). If it is neither, decline or exit.
Build skill stacks sequentially rather than pursuing a single 'perfect' role. Assemble 3-4 adjacent positions to create compounding competency.

When considering business ownership, honestly assess whether you have entrepreneurial tendencies. If yes, recognize the high risk/reward structure. If no, build sales capability as a more reliable wealth path.
Look to long-standing industries (insurance, oil, JP Morgan) as signals of structural profitability and durable margins. New industries lack survival proof.
Average churn rate across the most recent three to six months before using it in an LTV calculation; never use a single month's churn figure because monthly volatility distorts the result.
When a stagnant recurring-revenue business is deciding which growth lever to pull, fix churn first (improve product and client experience), then scale acquisition — not the reverse.

Use back-of-napkin LTV math to determine whether the current business configuration is growing toward an asymptote, shrinking toward one, or already at equilibrium — then choose the lever (sales volume, price, or churn) that most efficiently moves the asymptote to the desired revenue level.
Before attributing a revenue plateau to insufficient sales effort, calculate the revenue asymptote to confirm whether the current churn rate is the binding constraint rather than sales volume.

When building an affiliate referral program for a home-services or professional services business, design the offer so the affiliate would be stupid to say no — not a generic 20% kickback, but something that changes what they actually do in their business (e.g., a product they can sell at 100% margin, or a major commission that materially improves their revenue).

For a physician affiliate referral business, close the patient feedback loop with the referring physician immediately after the patient's visit: report on the patient's experience (without violating privacy), then ask 'Which patients did you see this week who would be a good fit?' rather than 'Do you have any referrals?' — the specific framing anchors the conversation to specific patients rather than an open-ended ask.

When transitioning a multi-avatar service business to paid acquisition, identify the one to three offers that convert most profitably as the front-door, then cross-sell and upsell the full menu after the customer is inside. Do not advertise all services simultaneously.
Never count the other person's money in an affiliate deal. Focus only on whether the deal economics work for you; what the affiliate earns is irrelevant as long as your unit economics are positive.

When introducing an affiliate or referral partner to your business, treat the first referral as a trial: the first patient or customer must be given a 'beautifully choreographed experience' because the affiliate is evaluating whether to trust you with their own reputation before committing to ongoing referrals.

For an insurance or commission-based sales organization that wants to scale, alternate content call-to-actions between end customers and prospective agents — the same educational content attracts both audiences, and dual CTAs allow double-dipping without changing the content strategy.
Reach out to 100 contacts per day for warm outreach, using personalized messages, following up up to three times per contact across multiple platforms (email, phone, DM, SMS, voicemail).
When starting a new product or service, make the first five deliveries free to get reps, collect feedback, build testimonials, and identify hidden costs before charging.
Ask for referrals at the moment of purchase, not later; include a three-way introduction request rather than just a name-and-number handoff.
Use only one call-to-action per content piece or ad; a confused mind does not buy, so do not ask audiences to simultaneously like, share, subscribe, and comment.
Before spending on paid ads, set up full tracking so you can accurately measure return on every dollar; launching without tracking is equivalent to playing a casino game without a budget.
Test one variable per week per advertising platform, log all test results, and only move to the next variable after four failed attempts to beat the current control on the identified constraint.
Give employees a finite, manageable lead quota each week (e.g., 70 leads for a rep who could handle 100) so they can work each lead thoroughly rather than burning through a large list carelessly.
Deliver progress updates and small wins as frequently as possible within the first 48 hours after a customer buys; customers form their lasting impression of a business in this window.
Structure cold outreach so that if someone asks you not to contact them again, remove them immediately; it is more efficient to convert neutrals to yes than negatives to yes.
Make content assuming the viewer has never heard of you; inside jokes and internal references slow audience growth because strangers feel excluded and will not share.
When entering a new market, start with a free or massively discounted offer to generate initial lead flow before adding friction or monetizing more aggressively.
Never structure a promotional offer so that free or discount changes the core product; treat it as wrapping paper around the same Grand Slam Offer.
If a free offer produces no response, diagnose which of the three failure modes applies (wrong product/description, credibility gap, or wrong targeting pool) before changing the offer price.
When using a discount front end, splinter the core offer into a small component piece to discount rather than discounting the full core offer, to avoid price-anchoring buyers at the discounted rate.

For service businesses with high-cost practitioner time, use the Proprietary 5-Minute Appointment Method: delegate the first visit to admin staff for paperwork and pre-qualification, and have the practitioner appear only briefly to confirm the follow-up appointment where the sale will be made.

To qualify free-offer leads without abandoning volume, add friction progressively: start with qualifications in ad copy, then application forms, then multi-step funnels, then forced video consumption before any CTA appears.
If new to a market or lacking strong conviction, use a free or deeply discounted offer to close initial sales, gather testimonials, and build proof before transitioning to premium pricing.

Match the entire acquisition strategy (price, prospect, process, promotion, product) to either a free-offer structure or a premium-offer structure; do not mix premium pricing with free-offer ad economics.

When a customer wins store credit in a Win Your Money Back program, offer to apply it as a monthly discount over 12 months (e.g., $600 credit becomes $50/month off a $200/month membership) rather than giving free months upfront; this keeps customers paying and engaged over the long haul.

Make all meetings and check-in calls a required criterion for winning money back in Win Your Money Back offers; these meetings serve as upsell opportunities and the best time to make the next offer based on the customer's progress.

In upsell sequences, always offer more profitable upsells before less profitable ones, and bundle multiple upsells into named packages (e.g., 'Total Transformation Package') to make a single ask that closes multiple items at once.

End every sales meeting by scheduling the next appointment before the customer leaves (Book A Meeting From A Meeting, BAMFAM); the next appointment is the most important upsell opportunity in a recurring service business.

In continuity offers, always present the option to pay annually or prepay multiple months alongside the monthly option; use bulk prepaid discounts to boost 30-day cash — only one in eight customers needs to take a 'buy five get one free' offer to raise 30-day profits by 50%.

When a customer wants to cancel a continuity offer, offer to waive the cancellation fee in exchange for an exit interview; Hormozi reports saving approximately one third of customers who agree to exit interviews by either solving the problem or rollover-upselling them to a higher-tier offering.

To reduce declined payments in recurring billing, align payment dates with customers' paycheck schedules; if a payment is declined, attempt to run it multiple times on the same payday to recover a third of declined payments.

When building a Giveaway offer, set the grand prize value high enough to generate genuine demand; a grand prize that fails to attract entries signals the prize was not grand enough, not that the giveaway format doesn't work.

In a Feature Downsell process, remove features from highest to lowest customer value; this causes customers to self-re-upsell as they realize how much more value the more expensive option delivers per dollar of additional cost.

When adding a 3% processing fee to recurring offers, offer a second form of payment (preferably ACH direct debit) to customers who want to avoid the fee; this reduces revenue lost to expired cards and processing failures while reducing the cost argument for the fee.

When listing problems for a Grand Slam Offer, map each problem to all four value equation dimensions: Does not work (dream outcome), Won't work for me (likelihood of achievement), Too hard/time consuming (effort), Too slow (time delay). The more sub-problems identified, the more opportunities to create perceived value.

Use the 10x/1/10th test when designing delivery vehicles: what would you provide if the customer paid 10x your current price? How would you still make them successful at 1/10th the price? This stretches the creative range of solutions and often reveals high-value, low-cost delivery options.

Never discount the core offer price when closing a deal; add bonuses instead. Discounting signals that prices are negotiable (permanently damaging perceived value), while bonus-adding increases value without conceding on price.

When using scarcity tactics for services, always sell out rather than over-supply. Announce the sell-out publicly so fence-sitters who missed see social proof that others committed. This stacks credibility and desire for the next opening.

Change ad creative (images/video) first when campaigns fatigue, then body copy, then headline/offer name, then duration and enhancer. Change the core offer structure only as a last resort after exhausting all wrapper variations.

Give every guarantee a specific, creative name and clearly state the conditional: If you do not get X result in Y time, we will Z. A guarantee without the 'or what' portion loses its persuasive teeth.

Frame benefits in copy from the viewpoint of how others will perceive the prospect's achievement (status framing), not just the outcome itself. Connect the dots: 'Your golf buddies' jaws will drop when they see your ball soar 40 yards past theirs.'

Create short-term emotional wins for clients as quickly as possible after purchase (within the first 7 days if achievable) to reinforce their decision and increase the probability they follow through to the long-term outcome.

When naming offers, use 3-5 components of the M-A-G-I-C formula (Magnetic reason why, Avatar, Goal, Interval, Container word). Keep it punchy and specific. Test 2-3 name variations simultaneously in advertising and measure response rate to identify the winner.

Commit fully to one niche before switching. Changing niches requires starting over from zero; the same offer in the same niche, iterated through enough attempts, will eventually produce a Grand Slam. Switching mid-attempt forfeits accumulated learning.
Devote one full day per week (e.g., every Friday) exclusively to ad creation using the assembly-line process: research and write 50 hooks, record 3-5 meat variations, record 1-3 CTAs.
Save all ads you encounter that you like to a dedicated album on your phone to use as a hook reference library on ad creation days.

Write hooks distributed across all five awareness levels (Most Aware, Product Aware, Solution Aware, Problem Aware, Completely Unaware) rather than concentrating them in the Most Aware (offer-driven) bucket.

When a CTA is identified that follows sound fundamentals (what to do, how to do it, when to do it, what they get, what happens next), stop testing CTAs and reuse it; a broken CTA can kill a campaign but a sound one does not need constant replacement.
Show and tell the CTA by visually demonstrating the next step in the conversion flow (click this button, watch the form appear, see the submit screen), not just verbally describing it.

When the existing ad pool is saturated and new hooks have also been exhausted, the next step is not new meat or new CTAs but expansion hooks that target a broader awareness level to reach a new audience segment.
Test meme-format hooks for the widest possible reach; for niche audiences use niche-specific memes that function as cultural in-group signals.
When scaling, double down on winning hooks by reusing them to generate additional variants rather than retiring them out of personal fatigue with the creative.
Give leads four scheduling options per hour (every 15 minutes) rather than one or two per hour, to increase convenience without changing appointment duration.
Offer inbound self-scheduling, outbound rep-set scheduling, and lead-initiated scheduling simultaneously; the more booking pathways available, the more appointments are booked.

On scheduling pages, use a Header-Headline-Subheadline structure (Avatar-targeted header, benefit headline, supporting subheadline) and display available time slots immediately on page load, visible without scrolling, on both mobile and desktop.

Contact leads in under five minutes of opt-in; the gold standard is under 60 seconds. If the team is not regularly hearing 'That was fast — you guys are on top of it!' at least once per day, contact speed is insufficient.
Use local-area-code call wrapping technology that dynamically matches the outbound area code to the lead's local area when calling; this significantly increases pick-up rates.

Use iPhones (blue iMessage bubbles) rather than SMS from business systems (green bubbles) when texting leads to increase response rates, as leads associate blue messages with real humans and green messages with spam.
Double-dial leads on first contact: call once, and if no answer, call immediately again. Many phones block the first call from unknown numbers and allow the second through.

Send automated appointment reminders at four intervals: immediately upon scheduling (include caller name, time, date, and the area code you will call from), 24 hours before, 12 hours before, and 3 hours before.
Send manual reminders from a real cell phone the night before, morning of, and one hour before the appointment, in addition to automated reminders.
Score leads on a 1-5 or red-yellow-green system based on qualification criteria derived from your top customers' demographics and actions, then route top-scored leads to top closers.
Initiate contact across all available channels (call, text, DM, email) but then continue communication exclusively through the channel on which the lead first responds.

Send personalized proof (case studies and testimonials) matched to the lead's demographics after scheduling and before the appointment, between the first and second call, and every 90 days for ghosted leads.

Track and publicly rank the sales team by show rate, close rate, and total lead-to-close percentage simultaneously; give cultural recognition (kudos, attention, approval) to reps with high show rates, not just high close rates.
Use an automatic dialer to improve lead-working efficiency 2-3x and ensure the team follows the cadence without relying on spreadsheets and sticky notes.

Build a culture of accepting unqualified leads as free practice rather than wasted time; treating every lead as a reps opportunity regardless of qualification drives skill compounding and prevents entitlement.

If you don't know how to create a specific value (e.g., increase e-commerce conversion rates), accept that you don't know how, commit to learning that skill, acquire the skill, and then you can sell it.

When seeking arbitrage opportunities or contract deals, talk to a large number of counterparties (e.g., building owners) to find the one outlier who is willing to transact at a significantly below-market price.

Be honest in affiliate recommendations; recommend products you have genuinely evaluated and believe in, positioning yourself as a time-saver for your audience rather than a self-interested salesperson.
Document partnership expectations in writing and ensure they are equitable and well-understood by both parties before any money or equity changes hands.
Test partnership fit by presenting both partners with the same data and asking whether they would make the same decision; if they wouldn't, relationship risk is high.

Before entering a partnership, clearly identify which of the three inputs (knowledge, money, time) each partner brings that the other lacks; if there is no clear differentiation, question whether equity is warranted.

When one partner has leverage in the early stage (e.g., availability, work ethic, capital), voluntarily offer more value than contractually required to establish reciprocity and prevent future renegotiation.
Evaluate a potential partner not just on professional qualifications but on lifestyle stability, financial habits, and decision-making patterns, as these will inevitably affect the business.

Sell supplements to fitness clients on their second appointment (nutrition consult), not the first sale. At the consult, bake supplements into their daily habits using an assumed close, then charge the card already on file.

When a co-founder or partner is not executing on their stated role, have a direct conversation that names the specific gap (you said X, we have Y) and states the consequence clearly rather than avoiding it or softening it.
When building a sales team, cut the script by roughly half; most scripts are twice as long as necessary, and simpler scripts get higher compliance and are easier to train on.
For high-ticket professional service businesses (e.g., dental implants), raise prices first before optimizing the offer or improving marketing, especially when demand exceeds capacity.
topic: Close Rate as Pricing Calibration Signal

text: For agency owners who anticipate clients bringing services in-house, pre-address this at contract stage by framing the transition path: move from done-for-you to consulting when they are ready, and stay on a consulting basis until their team outperforms your baseline.
For local paid social campaigns (Meta), plan to refresh creative every 21 days and build an in-house creative capability rather than relying on an agency for this specific function.
For local PPC and SEO, start with a specialist agency rather than hiring in-house; use the agency engagement to train an in-house person who will eventually take over.

When a sales team is underperforming, do not start with training; start with universal script enforcement. Only after everyone follows the same script does training or script iteration produce measurable team-wide results.

When evaluating a city for GMB entry, remove branded search queries (e.g., 'Joe's Plumbing Petaluma') and unrelated homophones (e.g., 'corn stock fence') from the raw keyword tool volume before using the number to estimate lead flow.

In the city research workflow, first scan competitor review counts across multiple candidate cities before checking search volume, because competition filtering eliminates more candidates and is faster to execute visually on Google Maps.
topic: Market Selection Criteria: Growth + Pain + Targeting

text: When naming a GMB business profile, use the exact keyword phrase with the highest monthly search volume for that service-city combination (e.g., 'Plumber Petaluma') rather than a branded or generic name, to maximize ranking relevance for the primary search query.

Familiarize yourself with your niche's typical close rate and average ticket before running city selection math, as emergency services have higher close rates (~50%) while high-ticket services have lower close rates — using the wrong assumption produces misleading revenue projections.

When expanding to new cities, collect and score 10-15 candidate cities before listing any profiles, then prioritize them by the ratio of search volume to average competitor review count to sequence your market entries by expected ROI.

Secret shop your own business before assuming the sales script is being followed; Hormozi recommends doing it because the gap between what owners believe is happening and what frontline staff actually say is typically severe.

When handling objections after a price is stated, use a head-tilt and childlike curiosity framing (e.g., 'huh, that's interesting — what changed between then and now?') rather than a counter-argument, to keep the buyer in explanation mode rather than defensive mode.

Train sales staff to say 'prepayment discount' not 'paid in full' — the former is a customer benefit framing, the latter is a salesperson's internal accounting term that sounds transactional to the buyer.

Build point-of-sale automation checkboxes that force script steps to be completed before staff can advance in the system, so that script adherence is structurally enforced rather than relying on memory.

Install the mantra 'everyone buys something' within a sales team to ensure that every customer interaction ends with at least the lowest step-down offer (rebook next appointment) rather than walking out with no purchase.

When transitioning a payment plan to recurring, automatically attach the recurring charge at the same price as the payment plan installment at the end of the program, so the continuity feels like a natural extension rather than a new sale.

Apply the diagnostic sales framework across radically different service verticals by identifying the current state, desired state, and obstacle for whatever the customer truly wants — the underlying goal, not the service feature they named (e.g., buyers of house painting want a fully weatherproofed house by a deadline, not 'four coats of paint').

Actively prune your brand's associations: decide which associations you want to strengthen and which to remove, just as you would pull weeds from a garden. Left unmanaged, random associations accumulate and dilute brand meaning.

When building a content strategy for a specific vertical, identify at least four to five specific problems and desires that avatar is experiencing, then produce content that addresses each one — this positions you as a domain expert before any paid pitch is made.

When selecting a brand-building niche, use the four-qualifier screen before committing: confirm the market is growing, confirm the audience has budget, confirm the audience is targetable via existing channels, and confirm they have active pain. Reject any market that fails on any single criterion.

Keep the core value proposition (the primary pillar) as the constant anchor across all content; any additional personal or secondary identity content should be additive layers, never displacing the pillar that the entire audience coheres around.

Evaluate every partnership, appearance, or endorsement decision as a brand-association trade: explicitly name who you will gain and who you will lose, and only proceed when the gained segment is both larger in number and more aligned with your target who than the lost segment.
Build and maintain a master spreadsheet of your best-performing content of all time, tagged by FAQ and objection type, so sales reps can pull and deploy specific pieces between calls.
topic: Show-Up Rate and Lead Nurture Optimization

text: In phases 1-2, post something recent and competent on your social profiles to pass the legitimacy check that prospects perform after discovering you through outbound, affiliates, or paid ads; this is the only content objective at that stage.

When hiring content vendors, explicitly override their instinct to optimize for reach and impressions; define success by avatar alignment and conversion-relevant engagement (saves, shares) rather than vanity metrics.

Look at your organic content for pieces that earn disproportionate saves and shares; transplant those hooks and headlines directly into cold email subject lines and paid ad creative as pre-validated tests.
Include a single, specific call to action in content rather than pitching repeatedly; keep the rest of the content pure value to sustain audience growth.
Move from vendors to in-house employees as you learn each platform; scale volume internally before attempting phase 5 active capture and creation.

When building a small business, identify which of the 13 competitive moat types can be woven into your business model from day one, rather than trying to compete purely on execution quality, because execution quality is easily replicated while structural moats compound over time.

To ethically implement price discrimination without the risk of customer backlash if two customers compare prices, slightly differentiate the offer for each segment (e.g., add a small perk to the higher-priced version) so you can truthfully state the two offers were not identical.

When seeking distribution partnerships as a smaller business competing against entrenched suppliers, offer perks incumbent suppliers cannot or will not offer: lower wholesale cost, a branded retail kit that moves more product for the distributor, or free on-site staff training.

When a business is operationally constrained by a single outside lead source, consider acquiring small agencies that serve your market rather than continuing to buy leads; owning the lead source means owning the media assets and the customer data, converting a vendor dependency into a supply-chain asset.

Think about business competition from a consolidation lens rather than a competitive lens: rather than fighting neighboring competitors for the same customers, explore whether acquiring or partnering with them would create a combined entity worth more than the sum of its parts.

Protect the first four to six hours of every workday for uninterrupted deep work; schedule all meetings from the end of the day backwards so that reactive obligations never consume the high-leverage morning window.

When diagnosing a business constraint, ask: 'Why can't we 10x this right now?' and enumerate every blocker; the most frequently named blockers reveal whether the true constraint is ads quality, sales hiring, or fulfillment systems.

Before scaling paid advertising spend, confirm that the product is generating net word-of-mouth growth (more customers joining through referrals than leaving through churn, with zero marketing) to avoid amplifying reputational damage from a mediocre product.

For each business function each quarter, identify one measurable improvement (e.g., reduce lead response time from 30 minutes to 5 minutes) and accumulate improvements across quarters rather than resetting the focus area quarterly.

Ask of your own product: 'If every person who used this immediately told the next person they talked to that day about it, how good would it have to be?' Use this as the quality threshold before scaling marketing.

To decline meeting requests without social friction, maintain a standing reason (a book launch, a company sale, a major project) that provides the requester with a face-saving justification for not being prioritized.

When editing any written or visual deliverable, apply sequential single-focus passes (punctuation, data, typos, content substance, visual consistency) rather than attempting to catch all error types simultaneously.

Use LinkedIn cold outreach to recruit experienced talent who have already achieved at a higher scale than your current operation, framing the ask as a growth challenge rather than a title or compensation negotiation.
When entering a new market or launching a new product, assess whether you can offer something an order of magnitude better than existing solutions; if not, defer entry until you can.
Collect swipe files of competitor ads and hooks continuously; review them in the same session you record ads to keep inspiration top of mind.
When presenting outcome statistics publicly, structure each claim as: percentage of people who achieve X outcome in Y time under Z conditions. Use the fewest conditions possible.

When testing a new advertising channel, mark progress by funnel milestone (clicks, opt-ins, right-fit opt-ins, show-ups, sales calls) rather than immediate dollar return; budget 6-12 months and roughly half a year's profit for the experiment.
Write approximately 50 hooks per weekly ad creation session: 40 recycled from proven winners (80%), 10 net-new experiments (20%). Record ads the same day hooks are written.
Ask what would break first if you 2x, 5x, or 10x the business; isolate and fix that constraint before increasing volume.
Assume every ad reader has no prior knowledge of you, is in a rush, and reads at a third-grade level; edit copy until it reaches third-grade reading level before publishing.

Sort your current customer base by revenue contribution, identify the top 20%, find the two to three psychographic/demographic/geographic/behavioral variables that cluster them, then restrict all new sales and marketing to that segment.
Collect customer outcome data at day 1, day 30, day 60, day 90, and end of program; improve delivery until the stats become compelling; then use those stats verbatim in marketing.

When applying the Kaleidoscope Process to a winning ad, try at minimum: changing background color, adding props, re-recording verbatim, reordering segments, adding visual filters, adding visual effects, changing font/captions, changing pacing, adding music, and reusing the hook with new content after it.

When deciding whether to expand market coverage, evaluate five directions in sequence before acting: up-market (higher-value, fewer customers), down-market (lower-value, higher volume), adjacent market (different business model, similar avatar), narrower (sub-niche), or broader (parent category).

Always start for free when launching any new product or service, including within an established company; use the free phase to collect testimonials, generate word-of-mouth referrals, and earn the right to charge by demonstrating results before taking money.
Talk to customers to solve every category of business problem: low ad conversion, page conversion, pricing confusion, product delivery failures; the customers hold all the information needed.
Before doing anything new in a business, ask why you cannot do 10 times more of what is already working; solve the constraint that prevents 10x before allocating attention to net-new initiatives.

Arm salespeople with a curated list of content pieces mapped to each specific customer objection or concern; when a prospect raises a concern, the salesperson sends the relevant content before the follow-up call rather than trying to overcome the objection verbally in the moment.

When implementing a price increase for existing recurring customers, send a price-increase letter that highlights new value additions, frames the increase as necessary to maintain quality, and grandfathers existing customers at the old price until a specified future date.

Collect proof from your business systematically: screenshot reviews across all platforms (Yelp, Google, Facebook), print them, and display them at volume in physical or digital spaces to communicate social proof overwhelmingly.

Ask canceling customers what it would take to make things right rather than immediately trying to retain them; let them vent, validate their experience more strongly than they do, and then ask the specific question about what resolution would look like.

In hiring, ask whether you are learning more from the candidate during the interview than they are learning from you; if the candidate is not teaching you something about the role, they are not qualified at the level required.

Offer an annual prepayment option as an alternative to monthly billing, paired with either a discount or an added guarantee; do not force it as the default but present it clearly to capture the 10-15% of buyers who will prefer it.

When thinking about scaling a business, look at all existing assets—physical space, team expertise, relationships, content—and ask what combinations of those assets could generate a new revenue line without adding net-new operational infrastructure.
topic: Fast Cash Plays via Underutilized Assets

text: When you find a book worth reading, read it multiple times — until you can teach its concepts to someone else — and build your own presentation or framework around it to retain and operationalize the material.

In negotiations, identify all four data points — your need today, your need in 10 years, their need today, their need in 10 years — and find the closest solution that satisfies all four; explain this framework transparently to the other party.

When someone more successful is making more money than you, set aside ethical objections to observe what they believe to be true about the world that you do not, or to identify false beliefs you hold that they have shed.

Before committing resources to any activity, ask: Is this worth doing at all? If yes — is it worth the time required to do it well? Only proceed if both tests pass; then commit the time required to do it at the great standard, not just the good one.

When feeling complacency creeping into your entrepreneurial cycle, recognize it as the precursor to the learning-through-failure stage, and seek to compress the time in the complacency phase by acting as if the failure phase has already begun.
Prioritize spending on books, courses, mentorship, and skill-building over consumption goods in your 20s.
Set up automatic transfers to a dedicated investment/learning account before the start of each month.
Maintain a pre-approved shopping list and do not purchase items outside of it.
Check your bank account balance every morning, no exceptions.
When considering a purchase, convert the price to post-tax work hours required and ask yourself if you would work those hours for the item.
Choose roommates who share or exceed your life goals and ambition level.
Optimize for location convenience (highway access, gym proximity, cheap food options) even if it requires paying more rent.
Take one-time experiences (travel, exploration) that are uniquely suited to your 20s, within the bounds of your investment account.
Never run an ad without a deliberate headline. Every ad has a headline — the choice is only between a bad one (written by default) and a good one (written intentionally).
Test headline and hook ideas by reviewing the first three seconds of organic content and competitor ads — visually and verbally — before writing new headlines from scratch.
Steal hooks across industries: adapt headline formats that are working in travel or weight loss and apply them to your own category.
Write down all product flaws and customer complaints, then claim them proactively in copy using the 'X [flaw] but Y [benefit]' structure before prospects surface them as objections.

For each benefit in your copy, apply the What-Who-When status extension: identify what the benefit is, who (family, colleagues, rivals) awards the resulting status, and in what time period (past, present, future) — generating multiple angles from a single benefit.
Enforce urgency and scarcity limits without exception: say no to buyers who arrive after the deadline or after the quantity limit is reached so that future scarcity is believed.

Always include a PS statement in long-form copy. Use it for: (a) a disclaimer of who the offer is not for, (b) a single-sentence recap of the core persuasion points, or (c) a trained reward for readers who always read the PS (jokes, fun content that occasionally carries the CTA).
In multi-step funnels, tell the prospect exactly what will happen at each next step and then deliver precisely that outcome, repeating promise-fulfillment cycles to compound future compliance.

Run all ad copy through a free reading-level tool and edit until it tests at third-grade reading level. Prefer common longer words over shorter but unfamiliar words (simplicity over concision). Use short sentences, active verbs ('he sprinted' not 'he ran quickly'), and few adverbs.

Describe the experience of the desired outcome rather than the outcome itself: instead of 'get more leads,' describe the moment — 'salespeople can't write down credit card numbers fast enough because customers are reading them too fast.' Show the future problem they would prefer to have.

Document and substantiate every result, transformation, and client you have helped. Volume of substantiated proof (reviews, testimonials, case studies) compounds into implied authority and long-term competitive moat.

For email/phone code verification attempts, use your oldest aged personal Gmail account or a trusted family member's long-established account; Google Workspace account status and Gmail storage purchases improve approval likelihood but do not guarantee it.
For instant verification attempts, use a different device (phone vs. computer) and different Gmail account for each profile creation attempt to avoid device-linking detection by Google's algorithm.
For instant verification scaling in lower-spam categories, recruit third-party profile creators via Facebook groups, Reddit, and Discord and pay them $25 per successful profile creation.

For video verification, prepare visual proof of: (1) current location with visible street signs, (2) permanent business signage, (3) business equipment, and (4) proof of management authority (e.g., cash register, visible name tag); ensure all visual elements are clearly visible in the submission video.

For service-area business profiles (versus address-based), video verification is significantly easier to structure because you need only show location proof relevant to service delivery, not permanent physical signage.

Set the Google Business Profile name to include the highest-search-volume keyword phrase (service + city) before the profile is established; the name cannot be safely changed later without risking suspension.
Use SEMrush Keyword Overview to compare monthly search volumes across keyword variants (e.g., 'roofing' vs. 'roofer' vs. 'roof repair' plus city name) before naming a new Google Business Profile.
Stuff the target service+city keyword into the profile description, product listings, and services tab descriptions to reinforce keyword relevance across all indexed fields.
Add authentic-looking photos of actual workers doing real work to the Google Business Profile; avoid AI-generated imagery which undermines credibility with prospective customers.
Add a website with a contact/lead form to each Google Business Profile so that prospects who prefer not to call can still convert via form submission.
Use a review swap with other local non-competing businesses: leave them a review in exchange for a review on your profile.
Install CallRail (or equivalent call tracking) across all profiles from the start to attribute lead volume by profile and identify which ones underperform.
Start with at least 30 reviews and a verified address in a populated area before expecting consistent call volume from a Google Business Profile.
Manage multiple Google Business Profiles via separate Gmail accounts to keep them cleanly separated organizationally.
When partnering with local contractors for drop-servicing, negotiate a 40/60 split (operator keeps 40%, contractor keeps 60%) as the baseline revenue-share agreement.
Before reading another book or consuming more content, do everything prescribed in the last piece of content you consumed. Only after you have acted on it should you move to the next.
When you feel sad or stuck, ask: what trade am I knowingly or unknowingly unwilling to make? List the specific, concrete consequences of making that trade to test whether they are truly unbearable.

If under 30 with no dependents and dissatisfied with your trajectory, work as many hours per week as humanly possible now. Get your financial oxygen mask on first (cover basic needs via any combination of jobs), then redirect surplus time and energy into skill compounding.
Extrapolate your past success in any domain to new domains: identify a time you worked hard at anything and use that as evidence you can apply the same effort and meta-skill to the current challenge.
When afraid of a decision, force the fear into the specific: walk through the precise sequential consequences one step at a time until you reach the actual concrete worst-case outcome.
Commit to one pursuit for at least 100 days before evaluating whether to change course. Decline all competing opportunities for the duration.

Before changing ad targeting or increasing spend to improve conversion rates, first check whether the three-variable math (lead cost, close rate, deal size) already works at the current conversion rate. If CAC is acceptable given deal size, the problem is not targeting.

When running a consultation-call funnel for a medically constrained service (specific insurance type, specific condition severity), include a scored question about eligibility criteria in the opt-in form and only show the scheduler to leads who pass the score threshold.

For services where the customer must hold a specific insurance type that is automatically granted at a certain age (e.g., Medicare Part B at 65), use the age criterion as the primary targeting variable in ad audiences and ad copy rather than trying to target insurance type directly.
Add funnel friction in this order when unqualified leads are wasting rep time: (1) ad copy and messaging, (2) opt-in form fields with scoring, (3) conditional scheduler access based on score.

Post the VA job on onlinejobs.ph, not free platforms; use the paid tier and specify full-time employment, $1,000-$1,500/month salary, communication/customer service/Google Sheets as required skills, and make a neutral English accent plus a voice or video recording submission non-negotiable in the job description.

Give the VA a written script for answering calls, a Google Sheet template to log each appointment (time, day, job price, contractor cost, profit, contractor contact, notes), and clear instructions before they start; do not rely on verbal briefing alone.

Create a Google Business profile for the service category (e.g., car detailing) in each target area, add photos and gather reviews, then let the profile generate organic inbound calls; no paid ads required in early stage.

When prospecting local contractors for fulfillment partnerships, look for small owner-operated businesses with low-budget websites and low public pricing; avoid large branded operations. Pitch the volume guarantee ('2-3 bookings a day') as the negotiating lever to secure below-public-rate per-job pricing.

Do not hire a VA until you are already receiving enough inbound calls to confirm the VA's monthly salary will be covered by the existing profit stream; use VA as a scale enabler, not an early-stage experiment.

For a CPG brand launching a new TikTok Shop product, seed the top affiliates with product approximately 10 days before launch so they can create content in advance, then coordinate all of them to post within the same 24-hour window on launch day to maximize algorithmic concentration signal.

Manage a TikTok Shop affiliate community via Discord with dedicated full-time employees who host weekly video calls, answer questions daily, and build real relationships with creators, treating affiliates as valued partners rather than transactional contractors.

For new CPG brands, launch TikTok Shop, Amazon, and retail channels simultaneously rather than sequentially, because TikTok Shop content will drive Amazon search volume immediately regardless of where the consumer intends to purchase.
Use Fulfilled by TikTok (FBT) for TikTok Shop operations to remove the need for a logistics team and eliminate the risk of shipping-related negative reviews counting against your seller rating.

When negotiating with influencers for paid posts, calculate your current Facebook/Meta CPM, then target to pay approximately half that rate per thousand views from the influencer, adjusting for US audience percentage and demographic match.

Start influencer program outreach with a TikTok Shop affiliate agency to learn the operational mechanics, then replicate and improve those mechanics in-house as quickly as possible to remove agency margin and retain institutional knowledge.

For CPG brand events and retail pitches, invest in relationship-building at trade shows (e.g., Expo West) even without immediate business outcomes, as relationships initiated at events can convert to major retail meetings 3-4 months later.

For a new consumer brand, define the target customer by a hyper-specific demographic niche (e.g., women aged 18-25 trying to lose body fat while lifting weights) before widening to broader gender or demographic targeting.
Set a recurring alarm for your target bedtime rather than only for your wake-up time, so that you enforce going to bed on time as the primary controlled behavior.
When attending an industry trade show as an early-stage founder, focus on finding and joining the community outside the show floor rather than optimizing for immediate purchase orders or meetings.
Use competitor brands already selling to your target avatar as a free source of proven messaging templates; study how they talk to your shared customer before writing your own copy.

For consumer health products targeting mainstream audiences, treat palatability (taste) as a non-negotiable product requirement, not an optional feature — if the product does not taste good, the health mission becomes commercially inaccessible.

In a multi-product portfolio where one segment dramatically outperforms others, proactively schedule dedicated face-time with partners in underperforming segments to address the perception (not necessarily the reality) of neglect.

After an entrepreneurial loss (an L), reset your internal scoreboard to zero the following morning — not negative, not behind, simply zero. Do not allow a single setback to reconfigure your default risk tolerance.

If you are young and lack a track record, get in shape and maintain groomed presentation before entering professional rooms — the physical signal substitutes for the credibility you have not yet earned.

In early-stage entrepreneurship, do the unscalable: personally DM customers, call 50 manufacturers, film 30 videos in a single day, train one customer at a time. Do not optimize; use excess founder time as the rocket thrust before scale requires systems.
Build something special publicly; do not invest time in networking before you have established utility. High-value contacts will arrive inbound once you have something worth noticing.

Define your current moonshot relative to where you are now, not relative to an abstract billion-dollar aspiration. Revisit the definition every 6-12 months and escalate it as your capacity and track record grow.

Set up a Discord server specifically for your TikTok Shop affiliate community before scaling your affiliate program; use it as the primary communication hub for product information, creator engagement, and relationship-building.
Allocate a dedicated product sampling budget as an upfront investment before launching a TikTok Shop affiliate program; send product to creators to generate content and test which angles convert.
When launching an e-commerce product with proven demand, launch Shopify, TikTok Shop, and Amazon simultaneously to capture cross-channel halo effects rather than sequencing one channel at a time.
Let TikTok Shop affiliates create content in their own authentic voice; do not impose brand-identity guidelines (colors, tone, production polish) on creator content for TikTok.
Use incentive competitions (e.g., branded prizes for top affiliates in the first two weeks of a launch) to drive concentrated effort from your affiliate network around new product launches.

Activate TikTok Shop's GMV Max tool to automatically amplify affiliate videos that are generating organic traction with paid media budget, converting top organic content into residual income for affiliates.

Build a personal brand as a founder through consistent public video content; strategic partners (retail buyers, investors) will use this content as a real-time character and credibility signal before engaging.

Deliberately invest in physical presence in locations (e.g., property, memberships, event attendance) where high-caliber entrepreneurs and operators regularly congregate across multiple seasons of the year, not only at scheduled industry events.

Prioritize in-person networking trips and events even when short (24 hours) over skipping them due to schedule constraints; the opportunity density of high-quality peer rooms is not replicable remotely.

When reaching out to local business owners for review exchanges, use a warm, peer-to-peer tone ("help support each other") rather than a transactional pitch ("leave me a review"). This increases response rate and reduces perception of manipulation.

Target outreach to local business owners across diverse service categories (plumbing, landscaping, cleaning, tree services, dog walkers, handymen, contractors) as long as they maintain a business profile that can be reviewed in return.
Test the review-exchange workflow yourself for 30 minutes to an hour before delegating to a VA, to identify any friction points and validate that responses are achievable before scaling.

When hiring offshore VAs for outreach, seek candidates at the $3/hour price tier on onlinejobs.ph, Upwork, or Fiverr. Higher rates are unnecessary for script-following work; do not overpay for this task type.

Provide VAs with explicit instructions, a pre-written script, and access to the necessary accounts (Facebook Groups, Reddit, email) before delegating; minimize reliance on VA judgment or creative problem-solving.
Track and measure review output per VA (target: 2-3 reviews per hour) to ensure productivity meets unit economics; replace or retrain VAs who consistently under-deliver.

Recognize the reputational limit of this tactic: it works best for initial review volume accumulation (first 40-100 reviews). Overreliance or scaling beyond the local business pool may attract competitor backlash or platform enforcement.

Use reviews as a lead-generation multiplier for service businesses: build multiple local business profiles for the same service category, automate review generation for each, and monetize incoming call volume via contractor arbitrage or service delivery.

When setting up a Google Business Profile for drop-servicing, use a made-up business name (e.g., Eric's Mobile Car Detailing), add photos of high-quality work from the relevant service category, and list a real phone number that you can answer immediately.

For geographic address on a Google Business Profile, use a real building address near high-income residential areas rather than your personal address; this controls your local map pin placement and targets higher-value customers.
topic: Geographic Expansion Sequence: Dominate Local, Then Expand

text: Use CallRail to purchase forwarding phone numbers for each new city or area you expand into; each Google Business Profile should have a distinct phone number to avoid Google consolidating or flagging multiple profiles.
topic: Geographic Expansion Sequence: Dominate Local, Then Expand

text: When negotiating with a contractor, tell them you are paying $60-$80 per customer in advertising costs even if your leads are organic and free, so the contractor perceives the margin split as fair and continues accepting your jobs.
Script your inbound call response using AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) to create a professional, repeatable phone script for quoting jobs and booking appointments.

Create a simple website ($15 or free) with visible pricing for your service to capture leads who want to research before calling; leaving a lead-capture form allows you to call back prospects who do not immediately phone.

Once making consistent revenue, purchase a full-time hourly worker via a job posting (e.g., on Indeed, ~$50 posting cost) to handle inbound calls and booking coordination, which saves time and scales throughput beyond what a solo operator can manage.

List your GMB profile at a physical commercial building address (not a service-area business listing), choosing a large building with many tenants so the address attracts no attention. You do not need to own or lease the address.
To find cleaners to outsource jobs to, search Facebook Marketplace, Nextdoor, and Craigslist for independent cleaners offering hourly rates; vet for own vehicle and own supplies before committing.
Use SEMrush's free keyword overview tool (five free searches available) to check monthly search volume for 'house cleaning [city name]' before investing in a GMB profile for that city.

Fill out all GMB profile sections (title, description, services, service area, products, Q&A, updates) with the exact keyword phrases customers search — e.g., 'house cleaning near me', 'house cleaning [city]' — to signal relevance to Google's local ranking algorithm.
When aiming to scale beyond $20,000/month in the remote cleaning model, hire a virtual assistant to handle all inbound calls so the operator is completely removed from customer interactions.
Acquire recurring customers by asking cleaners to offer weekly or bi-weekly plans on-site; store the customer's card on file for automatic billing so no manual collection is required.
Build a basic business website (AI-assisted website builders like Hostinger AI take ~2 minutes) and add a quoting widget so customers can get quotes online without calling, reducing friction.

Select a high-urgency service niche (pest control, plumbing, electrical) over recurring or lifestyle services when speed-to-revenue is the priority; urgency drives immediate inbound calls rather than requiring nurture sequences.
Include the exact service plus city keyword (e.g., 'Pest Control Scarborough') in the Google Business Profile business name to improve Map Pack ranking for that search query.

Use a virtual phone number service (e.g., CallRail at ~$50/month for five numbers) rather than a personal number for Google Business Profiles in drop-servicing, to separate business calls and track performance per profile.

Set up multiple Google Business Profiles across adjacent low-competition cities (e.g., four to five cities) simultaneously rather than one at a time, to aggregate search volume to the ~5,000/month threshold needed for four jobs per day.

Use AI website builders (Hostinger AI, Lovable) to create a functional service business website in under 10 minutes; website quality is a secondary ranking factor compared to reviews and GMB keyword optimization.

Use ChatGPT to generate keyword-dense Google Business Profile descriptions; input the exact service+city keyword and ask the model to use it as many times as naturally possible across the profile sections.

Find subcontractor candidates by searching Facebook Marketplace for individuals offering the target service; message them with a clear value proposition: 'I generate leads, pay all advertising, book all appointments — you just show up. 60-40 split.'
Verify payment integrity with subcontractors by calling the customer after service delivery and casually confirming the amount charged, without disclosing you are cross-checking the subcontractor.

Quote an inspection fee (e.g., $60) for pest control jobs that is waived if the customer proceeds with service; this creates soft commitment and covers subcontractor costs if the customer declines after on-site assessment.

Use Semrush keyword overview (free-tier searches) to validate monthly search volume for each city keyword before committing to building a profile there; target at least 600 searches/month per city for pest control.

When pivoting content to attract practitioners rather than end-consumers, lead videos with client case-study hooks ('here is a client who came to me with this issue') rather than personal experience hooks ('here is what I experienced'), preserving all existing story and expertise while shifting which audience self-identifies with the content.

If you teach frameworks and philosophies inside a paid training, make those frameworks and philosophies the primary substance of free public content; do not withhold them out of fear of cannibalization.

Before rebuilding a content strategy from scratch, diagnose whether the problem is topic mismatch (requires new content) or frame mismatch (requires only repackaging existing content); frame mismatch requires only a wrapper change, not a content overhaul.

For a hotline-style interactive content format in a coaching business, have aspiring coaches or existing practitioners call in to discuss client situations rather than having end-consumers call in to discuss personal problems; this filters callers to match the offer audience.

When afraid to take a risk, write down in step-by-step detail exactly what you are afraid will happen; make it as specific and concrete as possible to reveal whether the feared outcome is actually survivable.

Commit your effort completely to things within your control and then accept outcomes as they come; do not let uncontrollable variables (ad account shutdowns, internet outages, storms) become reasons not to commit fully to the controllable ones.
When setting a goal, make your commitment to the effort entirely divorced from the outcome; die trying rather than not trying because of what others might think if you fail.

Approach every component of your life — footwear, beliefs, politics, relationships — by asking two questions: what do I want? And does this thing help me get it? If you cannot explain why you believe what you believe, you have adopted someone else's belief without questioning it.

Frame contract discussions as protection against unspoken expectations: say you want everything in writing so there is no misunderstanding and so you cannot inadvertently disappoint the other party by failing to meet an expectation you were unaware of.
topic: Partnership Equity Must Be Codified Upfront

text: Discuss all key partnership contingencies before any money is at stake: what happens if either party wants to exit, if one party dies, if you disagree on profit distribution, if you disagree on whether to sell the business.
topic: Partnership Equity Must Be Codified Upfront

text: Read all employment agreements, partnership agreements, and laws applicable to your business and industry; ignorance of a law does not exempt you from its consequences.
topic: Partnership Equity Must Be Codified Upfront

text: Before reacting to a provocation or interpersonal conflict, ask: what do I want to have happen? Then ask: does this action increase the odds of that happening? If not, do nothing.
Limit yourself to one genuinely new business initiative per year; direct remaining energy to doing more of what already works and making small improvements on the current model.

When you have identified the true constraint of a business and begun solving it, give the solution time to work before switching course; do not abandon a correct long-term solution at six months because it has not yet produced results.
In marketing copy, sales pitches, and emails: use one big idea with ten reasons rather than ten ideas with one reason each.
Structure each bonus in an offer so that it is individually worth more than the total price of the entire offer.
Once you have mastered delaying gratification, deliberately decide when to begin reaping; do not defer indefinitely.

Use SEMrush keyword overview (semrush.com) to check monthly search volume for your service plus each target city before setting up a Google Business Profile. Choose the keyword variant (e.g., 'landscaping' vs. 'landscaper') with the higher search volume for that specific city, and use that exact term in your profile name.

Set up a Google Business Profile at business.google.com with a physical commercial address in the target city (can be any commercial building), verify via phone code for your first profile, and add a service area. The profile name must include the service keyword plus the city and cannot be changed after verification.

For website creation when launching a local service business, use an AI website builder (e.g., lovable.ai) rather than custom development. A basic functional website is sufficient to satisfy Google's requirement for a credible business presence; production quality is irrelevant to local pack ranking.

When onboarding a new landscaping or trade-service customer, book a free on-site assessment to perform quoting. Generate the quote using a CRM or ChatGPT, send a formal invoice or contract for signature, and collect a minimum 30% deposit (50% preferred) before any work commences.

To find subcontractors for trade or landscaping jobs in a new market, post job listings on Indeed or Facebook for laborers, or cold-call businesses that appear on page four and beyond in Google search results for the relevant service and city.
Increase the base unit of money you measure things in, starting with awareness of your current unit and intentionally shifting to the next higher tier (e.g., $1K → $10K → $100K).
Change your organizational default deadline from end-of-week to end-of-day (or even 4 hours from now) to compress execution cycles.
Intentionally hang around people who use larger monetary units, execute faster, and think in decade-long time horizons; allow their defaults to become your new baselines.
Practice delayed gratification and self-restraint on small decisions; build the impulse-control muscle that enables long-horizon goal setting.

When evaluating a new business opportunity, list the five things you believe will go right, then assume none of them will happen, and ask whether you still win; only pursue opportunities that survive this worst-case filter.

Eliminate idea risk before committing to a new venture by only targeting markets with established, durable demand (e.g., more customers, weight loss, higher income, entertainment) so that execution quality is the only remaining variable.

Calculate the risk-adjusted return of any bet by multiplying the payoff by the probability of success before comparing opportunities; prefer higher-probability bets when risk-adjusted returns are equivalent.

Build structural advantages (large existing audience, established brand, proven distribution) before placing any major business bet, so that the bet's outcome is less dependent on luck and more dependent on controllable execution.
Answer inbound calls with your name and company name: 'Hey, this is [Name] from [Company Name] speaking, how can I help you?' — this sets a professional tone that most local trade competitors lack.
If you miss an inbound call, at minimum send a text message back immediately; preferably call back. Missed calls that receive no follow-up are effectively lost to a competitor.
Charge a nominal inspection fee ($60 in Eric's plumbing example) that is waived if the customer proceeds with the repair; never give a price estimate over the phone for services requiring diagnosis.
When sourcing subcontractors, call approximately 10 local providers per trade and ask each if they will accept contracted work on a 60-40 split; expect roughly 3 out of 10 to agree.

To rank a Google Business Profile, verify the listing and accumulate reviews (Eric describes using fake reviews); add good photos; repeat the profile setup across multiple geographic markets or service types to multiply lead volume.
Schedule subcontractor visits for the same day whenever possible; same-day service matches customer urgency and enables same-day payment collection.

Install a lead nurture playbook (standardized pre-call communication sequence) immediately for any DM-funnel business with a sub-70% show rate; treat the show rate improvement as a near-zero-cost revenue multiplier before addressing other funnel metrics.
topic: Show-Up Rate and Lead Nurture Optimization

text: Before adding automation to the DM setter function, first increase raw setter headcount to ensure all leads are contacted; automation optimizes a working setter process but cannot substitute for adequate coverage when leads are simply not being reached.

When a business is running 80%+ margins, do not introduce lower-ticket offers in response to low overall conversion rate; diagnose whether the conversion problem is price-driven or operations-driven before touching offer structure.

Verify that a thank-you page video (VSL equivalent) exists between call booking and the sales call; this pre-frames pricing, proof, and positioning before the closer speaks, reducing early-call objections.
topic: VSL as Qualification and Pre-Frame Gate

text: When selecting a city to target for a Google Business Profile, use Google Maps to check the top-three organic results for your target service keyword. Look for at least two of those three profiles to have under 100 reviews. If one or more have over 100 reviews, check whether that high-review profile is actually your direct competitor (e.g., a landscaping supply store is not competition for a landscaping service provider).

Spam the target service+city keyword phrase throughout your Google Business Profile: put it in the business name, in the description, in every product and service listing, and in any other free-text field. This keyword density is the single most important on-page SEO action after achieving a sufficient review count.

To find subcontractors for your remote service arbitrage business, search Google Maps for the same service you are listing, contact those small business operators, and offer them a 60/40 subcontract split (they receive 60%). Also post on Facebook Marketplace. Frame the pitch as offering them a volume of ready-to-close jobs rather than asking them to negotiate.

When registering a Google Business Profile as a service-area business, use a real address in the target city for the verification mailing address field (any real address in that city works). Set the business up without a displayed address so it appears as a service-area business with a coverage grid rather than a pinned location.

To acquire reviews quickly for a new Google Business Profile, go to public places (malls, college campuses, parks, local festivals) and offer small incentives (candy, drinks) in exchange for a Google review. Also reach out to other local business owners via Reddit, Facebook groups, and Discord servers for reciprocal review exchanges. Hire a local helper (e.g., a younger sibling) to canvass on your behalf.

Scale the remote service arbitrage business by reinvesting profits into: (a) paying for reviews on new profiles, (b) hiring a Filipino VA at ~$5/hour from onlinejobs.ph to handle all inbound call answering and contractor coordination, (c) creating a website and improving it with SEO, and (d) entering new city markets with fresh Google Business Profiles.

Replace a generic request-for-quote opt-in form with a branded quiz (e.g., 'Perfect Entertainment Match Quiz') that asks five to seven questions about the wedding; route leads with sufficient budget directly to a booking calendar and send others to a PDF or no-book outcome.
Send the VSL before the sales call and include a secret word or data-request inside the video so the rep can verify the prospect watched it before the call begins.
In the VSL and at the start of the sales call, anchor the buyer's reference point to the largest spend categories in their budget (flowers, catering, venue) before stating the entertainment price.

When presenting a two-tier anchor upsell, fully commit to selling the premium tier before offering the lower tier; do not retreat to the lower price until the buyer has genuinely considered and partially justified the premium price.
Use an automated DM triggered on join in a free community as the first touch in the free-to-paid conversion sequence.
Frame your sales VSL as classroom modules (4 videos: intro + 3 core stories + offer reveal) rather than a webinar to reduce psychological resistance from sophisticated buyers.
Rotate pinned posts daily or twice daily; pin other members' posts rather than only your own to signal that members can achieve that recognition.
Send personal DMs to community members who make great posts immediately after they post; this reinforces the desired post type and escalates the poster's commitment to the community.

Reserve your community creator account for genuine engagement; have community managers post from their own accounts rather than the creator's account, because members join for the creator, not for the manager.
Add a group onboarding call for every new community member (even low-ticket); structure it as goal/obstacle/current-state discovery, which naturally surfaces upsell opportunities.

Talk to churned customers and retained customers separately; identify what churned customers did versus what retained customers did, then emphasize the retained-customer behaviors and remove the churned-customer friction points.

When diagnosing what to improve in a community funnel, find your most confused potential user (the functional equivalent of a stoner who has never heard of your platform) and write down exactly what they do not understand - that is the real problem statement.
Schedule all calls and coordination activities on a single day per week (maker/manager separation); protect all other days as deep-work maker blocks with zero meetings.

When testing price changes in a subscription community, compute LTV at each price (LTV = price / churn_rate) and conversion rate at each price, then compare EPC; do not choose the higher price or higher conversion in isolation.

For high-ticket community offers priced at $15k-$50k, choose the lower price that maximizes customer count when EPC is equal; more customers generates more word-of-mouth, case studies, and distribution value.

Give refunds quickly and without friction; Planet Fitness-style friendly goodbyes produce higher win-back rates than punitive no-refund policies, and zero-drama refunds prevent the customer from becoming an active detractor.
When facing a scaling problem, first identify the true constraint via Theory of Constraints; improve the bottleneck lever rather than working on preferred activities.
Niche down your service delivery to serve only the highest-value customer type instead of attempting to improve overall quality across all segments.
Choose the capital deployment path (partnership, acquisition, or licensing) based on your greatest comparative advantage and available resources.
When scaling from $10M to $100M, accept that you may need to take a half-step backward (e.g., shift business model) to enable 20 steps forward.
For high-reach creators, position as a viral-creative shop producing ads for paid media amplification rather than renting audience for direct sponsorships.
Identify the highest-paying advertiser category via pattern analysis, then acquire or clone a competitor in that space and apply audience reach to scale.

If you love the actual doing of the business—the product or service you deliver—start with the pure artist path. If you're good and truly love it, you should naturally beat competitors who don't love what they do and build demand through word-of-mouth.

If you just love entrepreneurship and don't care what you sell, focus on the entrepreneur path: find market needs, connect supply to demand, build organizational systems, hire an operator, and let it run for cash flow.

For the hybrid path, identify the component of business you love most—it could be product, marketing, finance, fundraising, or any key function—own that component, and have others build the rest around you.

When selecting advisors, prioritize those who have achieved your goal themselves and have repeatedly helped others reach it. Avoid advisors with no domain experience or vested interest in your decisions.

Focus on building an exceptional product first, then learn marketing second, then sales last. Do not optimize for short-term sales at the expense of product quality, as product excellence is the ultimate scaling lever.
Rather than spending heavily on paid advertising, invest in making your product so good that customers promote it for you unprompted, creating a compounding word-of-mouth loop.

When diagnosing a service business constraint, ask how much the bank account goes up monthly in cash (not EBITDA) to get a real picture of financial health, separate from accounting adjustments for equipment purchases.
Before adding new growth initiatives to a bandwidth-constrained founder's plate, first identify and remove everything consuming their time that is not the highest-leverage activity.
In a professional-services business, identify the most profitable service lines (in this case, weight loss and concierge medicine) and focus exclusively on those before attempting to scale.

Maintain an emergency fund (three to six months of expenses) before taking on aggressive investment risk, so that the psychological security of a guaranteed floor enables more offensive risk-taking in the rest of the portfolio.

Before deploying capital into any investment, understand exactly — step by step — how you would get your money back. If the counterpart cannot explain a clear exit path, treat the absence of a clear exit as a warning sign.

Align personal financial rules and business financial rules: if you do not take on personal debt, do not take on business debt; the same money philosophy should govern both domains to avoid cognitive dissonance that leads to drift.

When presented with an attractive opportunity, test whether it is your opportunity by asking: does this match my specific domain expertise and attention allocation? If not, decline even if the opportunity itself is genuine.

When evaluating an investment, convert the projected return into a doubling time (e.g., 'this doubles in three years') rather than an IRR percentage to enable cleaner intuitive comparison between alternatives.
Recoup your invested principal before deploying aggressively from remaining gains ('house money') so that subsequent high-variance bets cannot destroy the original capital base.

Disregard financial advice from people whose demonstrated financial outcomes are below your own target — regardless of their relationship to you (parents, close friends) — because their model of financial reality is calibrated to outcomes below your goal.
Measure and track monthly savings (income minus expenses) rather than monthly gross income as the primary personal finance metric, because savings is what is available for compounding.

Use business.google.com to create and verify your Google Business Profile; set the business category to match your niche (e.g., 'asphalt contractor'), decline to add a physical address location, and enter the service area city instead.
Use Semrush keyword overview tool to validate that your target city-niche combination has at least 1,000 aggregate monthly searches before investing time in profile setup.
Acquire a call tracking number via CallRail (or equivalent) before going live; set it as the profile phone number and configure call forwarding to the contractor's number.

To acquire initial reviews quickly: ask friends and family directly, purchase Gmail accounts and self-review, exchange reviews with other local businesses, or offer to pay for a stranger's coffee in exchange for a review.
