Require reps to submit three calls they found difficult before each one-on-one so the manager can diagnose the specific failure pattern in advance rather than diagnosing cold during the meeting.

Only move to the long-term career discussion portion of a one-on-one if the rep is hitting quota and their personal life is stable; if either is compromised, focus the entire session on the lower-level need.
When building affiliate relationships in service businesses with local referral networks, identify and recruit the natural gatekeepers and decision-influencers in your target market first.

For photography and event-based services, prioritize affiliate/partner channel development through targeted outreach to wedding planners and coordinators over paid advertising or cold outreach to individual consumers.

Measure outbound effectiveness not by immediate response rate or month-1 sales, but by pipeline maturity over 6-month horizons. Track the split of sales coming from direct response (month 0-3) vs. long-tail nurture (month 3-6+).

Build integrated nurture infrastructure (email sequences, content cadence, retargeting setup) concurrently with outbound launch, so prospects who don't convert immediately are automatically fed into long-term nurture streams.

For long-sales-cycle offerings, commit to outbound + nurture for a minimum of 6 months before evaluating ROI, assuming first-principles logic: 'More quality prospects in front of us = more revenue eventually.' Do not withdraw earlier based on short-term metrics.

Structure career progressions in two columns: one for title/perks (responsibilities removed at each tier) and one for compensation, alternating the type of advancement (pay one cycle, title next) to maximize the frequency of 'wins' an employee experiences.

Create in-house mini-certifications that gate access to higher-value work; ensure each certification unlocks both new capabilities (procedures, tasks) and measurably higher billable rates or customer pricing.

Apply the dual-column career-pathing model to any role with repeatable, measurable output—editors, salespeople, stylists, estheticians—by defining clear milestones (time-based or output-based) for each progression tier.

Use title progression in service roles to remove or reduce lower-value tasks (junior editors clean lenses, editors do not; junior estheticians offer only basic services, senior estheticians perform advanced procedures) to signal progress and make each tier feel materially different.

Use the court-filter test: when evaluating claims about behavior or intent, ask whether the statement would be admitted as evidence in court. 'You offended me' is not admissible (it's interpretation). 'John said X to Sally' is admissible (it's objective fact).

When someone describes themselves with a trait label (I'm disorganized, I'm an introvert, I'm bad at X), push back on the label by asking whether their actual recent behavior matches it or whether the label is outdated.

Evaluate friendships and peer relationships by asking: do they talk only about the past, or do they engage with future possibilities? Keep the peers who discuss your shared future; cut the ones dwelling in yesterday's accomplishments.

When receiving advice from family or peers, apply the 'alignment test': whose interests does this advice actually serve? Is it truly aligned with your goals, or does it reflect their worldview, their status incentives, or their risk tolerance rather than your optimal path?

Avoid asking people 'why' questions about their motivations or inner states. Instead, focus on observable facts: what did they do, what resulted, and what evidence exists? This eliminates post-hoc rationalization and reveals objective truth.

If you are trying to change a limiting label or behavior, consider changing your environment (who you spend time with, which communities you join) before trying to override the label while remaining in the social context that reinforces it.

Think of personal traits as continuums (how courageous, how organized, how patient) rather than binary states (courageous or not courageous). This framing enables incremental daily progress toward an ideal without the false ceiling of a limiting label.
Wake up every day and fight distractions again; do not assume yesterday's focus wins carry forward to today.
When evaluating an opportunity, explicitly articulate the downsides you cannot yet see; ask experienced operators about the bodies buried (downside realities).
When hitting the despair phase of a venture, physically create a visual representation of your position on the difficulty curve to contextualize that quitting at despair resets all progress.
To build a skill, execute the concrete action (cold calls, podcast episodes, writing pieces) in high volume before expecting mastery-level output.

If you are a young entrepreneur trying to build your brand, only create content if you are documenting real business activity and results. Do not transition into teaching mode unless you have proven results to stand behind.
When evaluating how to build a brand or replicate someone's success, study what they did to get there (the inputs, the work phase), not what you see them doing now (the outputs, the plateau phase).
Focus your early business-building energy on doing work worth documenting, rather than on creating a personal brand or positioning narrative. Let the work and its results speak for themselves.

After each objection-handling exchange, immediately re-ask for the sale: 'Does that help? Does that solve that for you? Great — are you ready to move forward?' Do not wait until all objections are addressed before asking again.

In the 24 hours post-purchase, proactively reach out to the new customer, confirm the specific goals they stated during the sale, map those goals to the three concrete next steps in your delivery process, and book the next meeting or handoff call immediately.

Apply the Rule of 100 daily: 100 minutes of content posting, or $100 in ad spend, or 100 outreach contacts — pick one or all three. Do not reduce volume because early results seem slow; the feedback loop requires sufficient data to reveal patterns.

Start every sales conversation by asking what specifically prompted the prospect to respond, comment, or reach out — use the triggering action as the opening question to surface primary motivation without cold-starting the conversation.

To activate affiliates in non-TikTok-Shop contexts, start a community group, invite microinfluencers you find interesting, announce a monthly ad spend budget, and split that budget proportionally among affiliates based on performance of their ads, creating a social structure that makes participation feel collaborative.

Before designing an affiliate program, audit whether your product is genuinely exceptional (not merely above average). If not, no affiliate strategy will overcome product mediocrity—invest in product first.

At the moment a customer is highly satisfied with a first purchase but not yet deprived of the next solution, ask for a referral instead of an upsell. Save the upsell ask for the moment they discover the next problem and become deprived.

In commoditized home service businesses, identify which of the three differentiation vectors (risk, speed, or ease) your business can credibly win on before choosing a positioning strategy. Conduct a discovery process comparing your strengths against competitors on each axis.
Pitch the maintenance plan at point of sale, not after project delivery. Use the future cost of repairs and resale value impact as the two primary closing arguments.

When structuring career paths for service roles, build six levels per role by alternating title/perk moves with pay bumps. Ensure each level requires a mini-certification or observable skill gate that justifies the promotion and increases the employee's ability to perform higher-value work.

Before opening a second business location, achieve scale zero at the first: remove yourself entirely from day-to-day operations and verify that revenue and margin hold for at least 30-90 days without your involvement.

Explicitly define and document the five vectors of your market expansion (upmarket, downmarket, adjacent, broader, narrower) and consciously choose which direction to move based on current skill level and competitive landscape.
Start a new business by artificially constraining the target market to a defensible niche where you can be the dominant player before attempting broader market penetration.

Clearly define your ideal customer profile, market segment, and geographic focus so that your messaging and positioning align with customer expectations and reduce confusion about your value proposition.
When introducing AI into business operations, isolate its access and set clear guard rails before granting broader access, rather than refusing to adopt or adopting without risk controls.
Apply Elon Musk's five-step algorithm to all business processes in sequence: question all requirements, delete the unnecessary ones, optimize what remains, accelerate, then automate.

Map your business as a diagram of input-output workflows rather than an org chart; identify which specific workflows each potential hire plugs into and which of those workflows could be fully or partially automated before making the hire.

To increase focus, list the twenty things you can remove from your environment rather than the twenty productivity hacks you could add; removal of non-target activity is the mechanism for better focus.
Add maximum friction between yourself and distracting behaviors (physical tokens, app delays, indirect posting tools) and lubricate the path to desired behaviors (remove everything except the task).

Curate your social environment by asking of each person: do they get me closer to or further from who I want to become? Move those who increase the distance further away and those who decrease it closer.

When setting boundaries with people whose behavior is unacceptable, do it without blame: acknowledge continued goodwill, state clearly that the specific behavior is no longer acceptable in your environment, and give the other person full autonomy over their choices.

Start process mapping at the high level (idea -> script -> shoot -> export -> edit -> post), then recursively decompose each high-level step into six or seven concrete sub-actions, continuing until each action cannot be reduced further. Only then identify which nodes to automate.

When specifying tasks for AI agents, use court-admissible observable-behavior language exclusively: eliminate adjectives like 'charismatic' or 'on-brand' and replace them with specific, measurable actions or detectable patterns.

Prioritize automating back-office administrative functions (invoicing, receivables, lead nurture) first for home services and brick-and-mortar businesses, as these are fully automatable with current 2026 tooling.

For businesses with sufficient cash flow, consider hiring a dedicated AI automation specialist to embed within teams, observe workflows, and continuously identify and implement automation opportunities.
Break down all business tasks to granular action-level steps rather than keeping them as role-level or project-level abstractions.
When training team members or GPs, focus on telling them what actions to take, not why or the theory behind the actions.
For each granular workflow step, create clear directions and assign ownership or automation rather than leaving steps implicit.
Document SOPs and productize services to remove founder dependency and enable scaling.

When evaluating a person's readiness for promotion, assess whether you still perform work that should be delegated to them—such as conducting tough conversations with their team. If you are, they are not yet a leader.
When hiring a C-suite executive, give high-level directives only (e.g., 'build out acquisition'). If you find yourself giving specific tactical directions, the hire is not C-level caliber.
Prioritize hiring for grit and capability over immediate technical skills. At higher levels, talent brings entire teams and established systems that eliminate ramp-up time.
Show up every day, regardless of enthusiasm or immediate results. This is the simplest and most powerful lever for success.
If you want to achieve a big goal, explicitly accept boredom and pain as prerequisites and plan for them; do not expect the goal to feel good.

If you want to develop a skill or build a business, work directly with or observe someone who demonstrates the trait you want to internalize (consistency, excellence, discipline) over months or years, not in isolated sessions.

When facing a supply bottleneck as a $200M+ business, first identify which businesses you bought developed land from over the past 10 years, then reach out to those developers (especially older ones with established teams) to explore acquisition or talent-acquisition deals.

Test hypothesis about whether developer relationships are transportable (whether the developer's brand and compliance relationships move to you) or extremely entrenched (zoning, local government relationships tied to individual person). If highly entrenched, acquire the company; if transportable, acquire the talent.
When diagnosing a revenue plateau, identify which avatar generates the largest share of revenue before deciding whether to add products or cut avatars.
After identifying the highest-value avatar, promote the one or two best front-end sales reps to handle back-end ascension exclusively rather than hiring new ascension closers.

For a niche selection decision between two adjacent verticals, test whether a single positioning statement covering both resonates with buyers from each vertical before deciding to split or combine them.
Once the model is simplified to a single avatar and linear funnel, shift all strategic energy to the question of what is preventing 10x more of the best avatar from entering the front door.
Analyze customer profitability by avatar to identify which customer segments drive positive unit economics; focus all marketing, messaging, and sales resources on that avatar exclusively.
Map fulfillment activities to retention and success outcomes; eliminate activities that do not correlate with retention and may even decrease it.

When service business margins compress as team scales, prioritize identifying the ideal customer profile (ICP) and operationalizing the business around that avatar instead of pursuing broader market coverage.

For subscription businesses evaluating billing strategy, consider prepayment (quarterly or annual) on new customer cohorts while keeping existing customers on their current terms. This captures cash flow improvement without retroactively changing existing relationships.

When acquisition channel is decaying or facing friction (e.g., cold calling becoming harder), the priority is expanding to new channels (paid ads, inbound, referral) rather than waiting for the failing channel to recover or changing the product.
For service businesses with high headcount costs, interrogate whether headcount can be reduced via AI automation before raising prices or pivoting to new markets.
Use a tool like oneof10.com to identify outlier YouTube videos in the same or adjacent topic space and model their thumbnail and headline packaging when creating new video content.

Script video introductions both verbally and visually; include physical props, attire, and environmental cues (e.g., lab coat, medical equipment, anatomical models) to reinforce the professional context and proof frame.
Structure every video introduction around four elements: Proof, Promise, Plan, and Pain (optionally) with at least one sentence per element to orient viewers and reduce early drop-off.
When running a content strategy experiment targeting a new audience segment, add an additional video per week for the experiment rather than replacing existing proven content formats.

Ensure all five CTA placement positions in a YouTube video are active (e.g., one-third through, end cards, description, pinned comment, community post) to maximize lead capture without requiring additional content production.

Review which YouTube videos are outliers in view count (approaching 1M) and identify the topic and format patterns they share; produce more content in those formats before experimenting with new topics.

Implement script-based selling with loops: when prospects ask clarifying questions, loop them back to the straight-line sales talk rather than treating objections as consultation opportunities; this allows junior salespeople to execute effectively without deep domain expertise.

When recruiting sales directors, prioritize sales training capability and culture maintenance over media-buying or domain expertise; use the Sales Handbook onboarding process (available at Acquisition.com) to train management hires on teaching methodology.

Monitor director span-of-control and split teams at 10 direct reports; when a director manages 15 salespeople, consider promoting one frontline rep into a second director role to maintain training velocity.

Before hiring, audit the current sales process for consultative moments that could be templated into script; high TAM constraints often indicate process leverage (scripting, looping objections) rather than talent shortage.

Before leaving a stable external job, calculate the incremental revenue required to replace the salary, accounting for ownership split and business margins, to establish a mathematical break-even threshold.

When considering leaving a primary business bottleneck (founder dependency), evaluate whether the constraint is truly external (tradesperson supply) or self-imposed (founder doing all discretionary work), as the solution differs.

If a business partner is the sole expert in a critical technical function, document their methods, train junior staff, or establish redundancy before the partner reaches retirement age to mitigate succession risk.

If you are transitioning an in-person service business to online, start by keeping your existing in-person sales process intact and simply switch your delivery to remote. Do not rebuild your acquisition channel until the remote delivery model is working.
For a brand-new online business with no audience, prioritize advertising and awareness above building or perfecting the product or course content.
Phase the transition to fully remote in two steps: 1.0 is in-person sales with remote delivery; 2.0 is remote sales with remote delivery. Do not attempt both transitions simultaneously.
When facing disagreement with a partner, ask for missing information instead of defending your initial position: 'What information do you have that I don't have?'
Ruthlessly prune new opportunities and business initiatives that fragment founder attention away from established revenue-generating businesses.

When running a five-day selling event for a membership, make the annual tier the exclusive offer during the event window, with clear annual-only bonuses. After the event closes, run a second cart-close phase with the monthly option ($27/month) but strip out 2-3 of the bonuses, keeping only 1 bonus to signal value difference.

If a prospect asks for monthly pricing during the event (or post-event), respond transparently: 'We offer monthly options, but you won't get these bonuses that I just spent time explaining, and they're valuable.' Do not lie, but you can make monthly less convenient relative to annual.

Track membership cohorts by launch month to separate stable long-term churn from early-stage cancellations; if your platform does not do this automatically (like Teachable), build a simple manual tracker or spreadsheet to follow one month's cohort.

Test adding a physical product to the membership offer in your next launch; even a single item (e.g., printer, sticker paper bundle) can justify a 2-3x price increase if it provides the end user with a tangible excuse to justify the purchase to a third party.

When hiring a high-leverage executive with a transition gap, establish regular contact and work dialogue immediately—do not wait for the official start date. Frame the pre-work period as opportunity, not imposition.

For talent-dependent businesses, prioritize recruiting world-class talent in production and strategy roles above near-term cost efficiency. The margin trade-off (slightly lower profit with a high-quality hire) is worth the bandwidth recovery.

In assessing whether to hire someone, evaluate them on intellectual parity and obsession with the domain. If they are not demonstrably better than the founder in their area of expertise, do not hire them for a C-level role.

Get up to speed on AI agents and automation tools like Make.com (successor to Zapier automations). Spend time building competency in ChatGPT and LLM-based agents so you can identify which 80% of your delivery work can be automated.

Track gross margin as the primary operational metric, not industry averages. Compare your performance against best-in-class competitors and your own potential, not against the average which is anchored to poor performers.

Frame AI automation as a market advantage and risk-capture opportunity, not as a threat. The agency that automates earliest will win margin and market share from competitors who remain labor-dependent.

When building a repeatable hiring process for a key role, map out the complete role definition, estimate gross profit per employee, and calculate the lifetime value (annual gross profit × expected tenure). Use this to set a recruiting budget as a percentage of lifetime value (typically 10% is justified for high-value specialized roles).

For one-off or non-repeatable hiring needs, do not build internal recruiting infrastructure; instead, negotiate a flat fee with a headhunting firm (typically 20-30% of annual salary) and pay it as a service purchase rather than an investment.

When facing a tight hiring deadline (weeks to months), activate multiple recruiting sources in parallel—headhunting firms, internal networks, LinkedIn recruiter, job boards—rather than relying on one sequential process. Plan to oversample (hire above your target) and filter for retention and fit.

Treat hiring spend as a capital-allocation decision using the lifetime-gross-profit-to-cost-of-acquiring-talent (LGPF/CAT) ratio, just as you would evaluate customer LTV-to-CAC. If the ratio is >5:1, the hire is economically sound regardless of the upfront spend.
For mid-tier and junior talent acquisition, run paid job ads using the same marketing funnel discipline as customer acquisition: test headlines, optimize copy, improve offer structure.
When pricing enterprise clients, test incremental price increases ($5k at a time) in each sales meeting to find the market-clearing price without triggering buyer perception of instability.
Position a media or distribution business against alternative media companies (Meta, Google, traditional ads) rather than against competing agencies or service providers.
For enterprise clients, use revenue-per-earned-media or CPM comparisons instead of direct attribution when sales are influenced by multiple non-measurable sources.
Acquire top-tier talent (director level and above) through outreach and headhunting, not job boards.
When a founder is constrained by dual roles (COO + sales), remove them from the sales function and hire dedicated salespeople to manage the lead flow they have already developed.
Establish a recruiting and compensation strategy for sales staff as a formal organizational function (career path, recruiting, onboarding, management) rather than ad hoc hiring.
Use the team-scale analogy: if you have a five-person sales team and add another five, the business can compete and scale at 2x pace, with each salesperson capable of five calls per day.

Track performance metrics (conversion rate, revenue per IP, audience quality) systematically across every licensed IP drop to build predictive data that improves negotiation leverage and reduces future volatility.

Test the ambassador program model by recruiting micro and nano creators in the anime community and running weekly drops for both their personal brands and premium IP, measuring which creators drive the strongest revenue and retention.
Reframe the acquisition strategy away from large media distribution companies (who view $4-5M exits as de minimis) toward strategic acquirers or alternative outcomes like licensing portfolio sales.
Use a keyword research tool to identify broader, problem-aware and solution-aware search terms adjacent to your core product keywords before declaring that a paid-search channel is saturated.

For visually differentiated high-ticket products, send customized product samples to relevant influencers in exchange for tagged content, then whitelist the best-performing content on Instagram and Meta.
For service businesses with excess profit above personal living costs, allocate that profit first to talent upgrades and second to brand-building activities rather than personal income extraction.

Treat failed ad keyword tests as sunk discovery costs in the search for scalable keyword clusters, not as losses; expect to spend $200k-$300k in testing to unlock the next growth tier of a paid-search channel.

When training on-camera salespeople, replace all trait-based feedback words (energy, charisma, confidence) with specific observable physical behaviors — raise your voice, talk faster, shoulders back — so the trainee has unambiguous instructions to execute.

For a live-selling business scaling past $6M, hire a finance person capable of forward-looking cash-flow forecasting tied to inventory purchase cycles and target growth rate, rather than relying on an accountant who reports historical cash balances.

To acquire on-camera live-selling talent quickly, recruit from the pool of micro-influencers and Amazon affiliates who already conduct live streams, and sign them to a fixed-term exclusivity contract to sell under your brand rather than their own.

Keep top individual-contributor salespeople in their selling role. Do not co-opt them as managers or trainers unless they have received explicit management training, because their management behavior will lag behind their current selling behavior.

Evaluate all in-house operations against the question: is this a competitive differentiator, or could a specialist do it better? Outsource anything that is commoditized to free founder and leadership attention for the core value-creation layer.

Test multiple acquisition channels before scaling ad spend on a single platform: explore micro-influencer partnerships, B2B wholesale to relevant professionals (e.g., dentist offices for dental products), and direct partnerships with category experts.

Diagnose whether a competitor's market dominance stems from product quality, reviews/social proof, a back-end upsell funnel, or multi-channel distribution before assuming they are simply outspending you on the same channel.

Focus product improvement efforts on the attributes that drive Amazon conversion: customer reviews, perceived quality relative to price, and complementary product ecosystem before investing heavily in paid acquisition volume.
Separate outbound (door-knocking) and inbound (lead-fed) sales teams structurally; do not feed qualified leads to reps who have not proven they can close cold prospects.
When testing a new sales channel or lead source, start with one proven closer and iterate on offer/lead quality; adding multiple new hires multiplies iteration variables and obscures the bottleneck.
Hire a competent full-time marketing director rather than using agency contractors for core go-to-market strategy; full-time ownership compounds better than per-engagement contractor services.
Test purchased leads in isolation with controlled variables; reject neither door-knocking nor inbound leads categorically based on founder belief.
Design inbound sales comp structures differently from outbound (lower per-deal %, higher volume stability) to account for the reliability and risk profile of pre-qualified lead work.
Run paid traffic directly to your About page rather than using a lead magnet landing page when your avatar is clearly defined.

Shift life-expectancy expectations downward to historical baselines (30-35 years) to increase gratitude for reaching modern ages. Use Jesus's 33-year lifespan as a reference point for significant achievement within a short timeframe.

Use the $100 Million Scaling Roadmap diagnostic quiz at acquisition.com/roadmap to identify which of the 10 growth stages your business occupies and the top priority functions (product, marketing, sales, customer success, recruiting, IT, HR, finance) for your stage.
Book a call with Acquisition.com to assess scaling constraints in your business and receive personalized in-person guidance in Vegas if your business qualifies for their portfolio support.

Maintain a cash-only wallet and replenish it only as income arrives; use the wallet as your de facto spending budget and avoid other payment methods (credit cards, bank transfers) that obscure the real cost of spending.
Before any purchase, convert the dollar cost into hours of work at your post-tax hourly rate, then ask yourself: would I voluntarily work that many hours just to acquire this item?
Apply the 'buy it twice' heuristic as a capital-allocation gate: only acquire items or services if you can afford to do so repeatedly or if the acquisition compounds over time.
Evaluate every relationship using the question: is it more likely or less likely that I hit my goals with this person in my life?
Remove people who accept you as you are; keep people who force you to grow.
During periods of isolation and group transition, focus on consuming aspirational content (podcasts, tweets, videos) to reinforce your vision of the future self.
If you feel pressure to walk a path designed by someone else, accept that one dream must die—either theirs or yours. Do not wait for permission to leave.

When you cannot articulate why you haven't started, pay attention to the emotional constraint (fear, shame, uncertainty intolerance), not the resource constraint (missing money, missing knowledge, missing connections).
Name the fear using the label 'coward' to yourself; the shame of that label is a more powerful motivator for action than the shame of 'afraid'.

Accept the worst-case outcome (permanent family rupture, permanent failure, public shame) before making a decision that defies inherited expectations; only after accepting the worst can you move forward with conviction.
Take the first step despite fear; observe that the feared catastrophe does not materialize, and use that observation to update your belief about the actual magnitude of the risk.
Ignore critics who lack direct experience with the risk or path you are pursuing; do not let social deterrence from average performers redirect your effort.
When seeking advice, deliberately seek out people who are closest to your specific goal — not those who are emotionally closest — and weight their input proportionally higher.
When expanding service businesses across state lines via partnerships, hire local licensed practitioners instead of trying to obtain multi-state licenses yourself.
When acquiring other practices, structure deals to buy majority control so you can enforce your execution standards without ongoing dependence on the other party's willingness to cooperate.
To reduce operator risk in a practice you don't personally license, ensure the structure includes three or four dentists rather than a single operator.
Raise price on education upfront or convert to an annual billing structure to appropriately value information; keep community/call access as a smaller, lower-priced recurring element.
Separate your product offering into consumable (recurring, lower price) and one-time (upfront, higher price) components; bill each component according to its true recurrence and value lifecycle.
When billing for community, calls, or services, price them as recurring add-ons only after the customer has completed the one-time education phase.

For a wholesale business serving stylists, run a front-end offset offer to get new stockists to activate their own client base on extensions; this converts stylists from buyers into advocates by demonstrating that extensions generate more revenue for their salon than traditional cut-and-color services.

Before evaluating a pivot to a new business model, ask whether the core constraint of the existing business (margins, acquisition) has been addressed first; if not, solve those constraints before considering any model change.

For an e-commerce or wholesale consumable business, demonstrate revenue retention by tracking cohort re-purchase rates rather than claiming the model is recurring; the data is what produces the valuation premium.

Walk your office space daily; observe energy level, cleanliness, organization, and mood to diagnose culture health before it deteriorates. Look for chaos, dirt, and filth as leading indicators of management problems.

Make unscheduled drive-by interactions with employees: brief smiles, shoulder touches during difficult moments, quick comments on personal hardships shared in status updates. Do not script these; keep them spontaneous.
Invest in subsidized or free in-office meals; remove price barriers to encourage employees from different functions to eat together, breaking down silos and building cross-functional relationships.

Require all employees to work in the physical office by default; make remote work the explicit exception, not the norm, if you believe trust and unstructured learning are central to your business model.

For early-career employees (age 18-35), prioritize in-person roles and proximity to adjacent functions; design onboarding to expose them to cross-functional activities, hallway conversations, and informal learning opportunities.

For recurring revenue businesses with strong organic lead generation, model the maximum top-line revenue possible at full advisor utilization (not with new hires) to establish a floor on future growth without acceleration.

When evaluating growth rate increases beyond organic hiring velocity, ask the Keith Cunningham risk filter: What is the upside, what is the downside, and can I live with the downside? If the downside includes business loss or reputation damage, do not proceed unless the upside risk is asymmetrically large.

In advisory or service businesses where new hires have a 6-8 month break-even period, structure upfront payment plans (e.g., $10,000 initial plan credited against first-year fees) to pull cash forward and reduce the hiring-rate constraint on growth.

Prioritize service reputation and organic lead generation quality above growth-rate speed, particularly when lead flow exceeds advisor capacity; losing reputation can close doors that would otherwise stay open indefinitely.
When considering a transition from 1-on-1 to group delivery, start with semi-private group sizes (6-7 people) before scaling to larger group formats if emotional or operational friction arises.

Do not scale a high-ticket offer by pivoting to low-ticket models solely to reduce founder delivery time; instead, restructure the delivery format (1-on-1 to group) while maintaining price point and positioning.
Spend the first 12 months in 1-on-1 delivery deliberately, extracting core problem patterns and solution methods, before productizing into group or scalable formats.

Stop using the word 'should' in internal dialogue and in how you listen to others' advice. Notice where 'should' appears (about school, career, marriage, lifestyle, rest) and ask: 'Is this my authentic desire, or someone else's expectation?' Replace 'should' with 'I choose to' or 'I choose not to.'

Use your own happiness and reinforcement as the measurement for whether your life choices are working, not external definitions of balance, health, or moderation. If you feel good, you're getting reinforcement, and the outcomes are meeting your goals, your life is working.

When you notice yourself dismissing someone else's life choice (as 'unbalanced,' 'unhealthy,' 'unsustainable'), pause and ask: 'What delta am I experiencing between their outcomes and mine? Am I dismissing because it truly is wrong, or because I'm defending my ego against my own competing desire?'
topic: Shame vs. Guilt: Navigating Social Signals

text: Spend time thinking about your own mortality and finitude. Use this frame to clarify which choices are authentically yours and which are internalized external expectations. Let the awareness of limited time dissolve deference to others' judgments.

If you enjoy working and are getting reinforcement from it, work until your output drops, then take breaks in whatever way actually restores you (even if it's not the 'approved' recovery method). Trust your own feedback loop about when work is healthy vs. unsustainable.
topic: Work as Identity and Capability Formation

text: When facing a moment of doubt ('why do I even bother?'), remind yourself: this is where most people stop, and this is why they don't win. The wall is the championship moment.
Measure your work output not by how much you do when motivated, but by how much you do after motivation fades. This reframes the metric from 'activity while enthusiastic' to 'effort under stress.'
topic: Discipline as Consistency with Disliked Tasks

text: When hiring, be explicit about discomfort and learning curves. Set expectations that work will be painful and unpleasant at times, and that this is a feature, not a bug, of growth.
topic: Leadership Sets Culture; Culture Determines Acceptable Effort

text: Use what you have — in the early stage, time is your only asset, so deploy it completely. Do not wait for capital, leverage, or more favorable conditions before starting.
When you catch yourself in a blame or grievance cycle about why progress is slow, deliberately shift focus to the single next available action: 'What can I do now?' Repeat this hourly.
Eliminate plan B options deliberately so that the primary path receives full cognitive and behavioral allocation. Acceptable retreat options reduce the intensity of effort on the primary path.
Read books, attend seminars, join communities of others in your industry, and save money to access mentorship — treat learning as a mandatory operating cost of the early stage, not a luxury.

Do more volume than other people in your chosen domain. The compounding returns of increased output (more attempts, more feedback, more wins) create an addiction to the cycle that sustains high performance.
Build proof of the results you teach; separate yourself from the educator swamp by demonstrating that you're worth more money and better at the game you claim expertise in.
Expect to surrender things at each stage of business growth that you weren't willing to give up when you started; frame this as the learning mechanism, not a loss.

When you claim you cannot learn something, set a 20-hour timer and commit to deliberate practice for the full duration before reassessing. Most perceived learning impossibilities resolve into mere lack of attempted hours.

Measure yourself only by the amount of action you take (input), not by how much you want the outcome, how deserving you think you are, or how hard you believe you are trying. Reality is indifferent to anything but what you do.

If you find yourself claiming the 'demon card' of having been through hard times, prove it by being hard now in your current situation. Use the frame that others have endured worse, therefore you can endure your current challenge.
Reframe entrepreneurship explicitly as an infinite game where not quitting is the only winning condition, not as a finite game where you are trying to outperform competitors at a defined moment.
Eliminate quitting from your choice set: ask yourself what the cost of returning to your starting point (failure) would be, and use that reframing to make persistence your only natural option.

When facing early-stage difficulty, reframe struggles as skill-building investments ('arrows in the quiver') rather than painful distractions. The resources and context you gain from solving them at this stage will asymmetrically advantage you when facing much larger challenges at scale.

Recognize that early-stage limitation (no one can learn for you, no one can work out for you) means the founder must personally invest time in acquiring skills and knowledge; lean into this period as a mandatory apprenticeship rather than resisting it as inefficient.
Throw emotions and spiritual-energy claims out of your decision-making framework; focus only on what did you do.
Eliminate everything that is not the core action you need to take; ruthlessly prune distraction and secondary considerations.
Use mental tricks to sustain effort: comparison to historical hardship (e.g., slaves worked seven days a week, so can I) and catastrophizing the alternative path (vividly imagining failure outcomes).
When stuck, explicitly think through the pain you will experience if you continue inaction, and compare it to the discomfort of the action you are avoiding; use the gap to create urgency.

When facing work you dislike, explicitly adopt a narrative frame that connects the work to a larger purpose (family provision, lasting creation, skill development) rather than focusing only on the task itself.

Double down and develop mastery in a high-leverage skill (sales, negotiation, communication) before diversifying into secondary interests; the primary skill creates optionality and leverage for all future work.

Use discretionary time blocks (early morning, evening, weekends) to learn and practice secondary skills while maintaining peak cognitive hours for primary income-generating work; this avoids the false choice between financial survival and skill development.

Recognize that passion-driven work will still consist mostly of unglamorous operational tasks; accept this and focus on mastery and meaning in the operational work itself, not on waiting for the 'fun' part to materialize.

When diagnosing why a business cannot 10x output, ask: what stops us from doing ten times what we currently do? Then trace every offered answer to its root cause by continuing to ask why until you hit the actual constraint.

Before automating any process, first question every requirement, then delete all unnecessary steps, then optimize the remainder for the best people doing the highest-return activity, then accelerate the timeline — only then automate.
As a leader, run a weekly 5-15 minute check-in with each direct report asking only: what is your number one issue? Help them solve that one thing and nothing else.

When evaluating whether to spend on cameras, equipment, or production quality for educational content, test with an iPhone first and measure performance — invest in production quality only after confirming it moves the relevant metric.

To get your first paying clients when you have no social proof: offer the service for free or in exchange for a charitable donation (at the price you intend to charge later), require the client to let you document their results, and accumulate 10-15 strong before-and-after cases before transitioning to paid.
When starting a service business, identify what people already ask you to do as a favor — that informal demand is the signal of what you can later charge for.

When building toward a business, minimize personal living expenses to the point where your savings give you at least 12-24 months of runway, freeing you to prioritize learning over income during the skill-accumulation phase.
Before launching in an industry, cold-contact operators in that industry offering to work for free or cheap; use the access to learn the operational mistakes others have already made and paid for.

When transitioning a client from free or charity-based service to paid, frame the ask as the same dollar amount going to a different recipient — not as a new expense — to preserve the price reference point already established.

When producing IRL or live-stream content, prioritize raw, unedited footage that captures real-time moments including technical failures and unexpected events, as audiences perceive imperfection as authenticity proof.
Extract and repackage long-form IRL streams into short-form clips to increase total content distribution across platforms, multiplying reach without proportional production cost.
Broadcast in-person conversations and social moments live rather than recording for post-production, to leverage the authenticity signal that unscripted, unpredictable real-time content generates.
Ask yourself: am I overcomplicating this? Is there a simpler way? When pursuing goals, actively check whether you are doing more than necessary.
Define what a perfect day looks like for you personally, then optimize for living as many of those days in a row as possible rather than chasing external outcomes.
Before committing to any major business or personal decision, ask: what problem are we solving? Different problem statements require different solutions and different personal costs.
When learning from successful people, focus on what they were doing during their climb to success, not what they are doing now at the summit.
Eliminate routines and habits that do not measurably increase your output, regardless of how they make you feel.
Before adopting a habit attributed to a successful person, check for counterexamples: other successful people without the habit, and unsuccessful people with the habit.
Evaluate your friendships by asking: does this person increase or decrease my probability of hitting my goal? If the answer is that they decrease it, remove them from your circle.

Rather than managing the emotional reactions of people who disapprove of your goal-driven behavior change, focus on the observable outcomes of that disapproval. If the outcome is that they avoid you more, recognize that as aligned with your goal of having more time.

Distinguish between actual friends (people committed to your goals and success) and people who are just there because of proximity or habit. Have the difficult conversation if the distinction becomes clear.
Implement three parallel conversion mechanisms within the free community: onboarding calls, a five-module self-serve video course, and weekly group calls.
Manually work free community members as leads before automating follow-up sequences, especially in early-stage community businesses.
Structure free-community courses as video sales letters with origin story, three case studies, and clear CTA rather than generic educational content.
When paid-media results decline, diagnose whether the constraint is audience pool depletion (widen to cold outreach or build free community) versus offer/creative issues before pivoting pricing.

Access the 10-stage revenue scaling roadmap by visiting acquisition.com/roadmap and entering your information to receive a detailed breakdown of all eight business functions, constraint symptoms, and proven graduation steps.

When re-evaluating an investment in a company where you missed an earlier, cheaper entry point, acknowledge the sunk cost of your earlier decision-not-to-invest rather than hoping the company fails (which suggests cognitive dissonance about the missed opportunity).

Periodically re-assess your capital-allocation framework: wealthy individual investors often need to shift from seeking 'cigar butt' bargains (companies priced cheaply that still generate returns) to acquiring exceptional companies at fair or expensive-feeling prices, as the latter typically deliver higher absolute returns.

Define your personal financial freedom number (the point at which additional money no longer changes your life or behaviors) and commit to recognizing it when achieved, rather than perpetually chasing higher targets.

Explicitly grant yourself permission to use earned freedom (time, resources) for activities that are personally meaningful rather than optimized for additional income growth once financial freedom is achieved.

Periodically reassess your life priorities across multiple domains (business, health, relationships, personal growth) and rebalance toward the domains where incremental effort yields the highest life improvement.
Identify specific, attainable stopping points for goals (e.g., physical fitness targets) rather than pursuing indefinite growth in domains where additional returns diminish.
Begin every book, contract, and important communication with a recitation of defined terms. Make precision about what you want and what you mean non-negotiable.
When defining success, define what a win looks like, what success looks like, and what a fail looks like explicitly, down to granular observable behaviors.
In sales conversations, replace metaphors and abstract language with observable definitions of what you are asking the customer to do or decide.
When communicating a goal or expectation, ask the other person to translate it into observable behavior ('If I do X, can you observe that?') to ensure mutual understanding.
Focus on variables in the sales process that can be observed and measured; ignore factors that cannot be directly measured or influenced.
Devote 4 hours daily to meditation practice to maximize the rate of subjective well-being improvement toward the 3-4 standard-deviation threshold achievable by advanced practitioners.

Spend time in contemplation of whether your life's primary goal should be external achievement (business, relationships, status) or internal well-being, recognizing that some goals (family, material security) can only be achieved at certain life stages and should be front-loaded before shifting to internal practices.

If you are a maximizer or high-agency individual, frame major life decisions (including meditation investment) as capital-allocation problems with explicit ROI and time-horizon analysis, rather than relying on inspiration or emotional conviction.
Identify what your best days have in common and arrange your life to maximize the number of consecutive days matching that pattern, rather than chasing happiness as an abstract future state.
Eradicate unconditional 'should' statements from your internal and external language. Replace them with conditional, goal-anchored framing ('if you want X, then Y is a higher-probability path').

Set explicit expectations with a partner before committing to a relationship about the primacy of your work, so both parties enter with aligned expectations rather than negotiating constraints retroactively.
Work at maximum sustainable output until fatigue causes a precipitous output drop, then rest; use felt energy as the scheduling signal rather than calendar convention.
When evaluating competitive position, assume the competitor has unknown capabilities and is a potential threat, regardless of apparent market dominance or resource disparity.
Always prepare extensively for competitive encounters (pitches, negotiations, presentations), treating visible preparation effort as a net positive, not as an admission of lower natural talent.
Frame yourself and your organization as the underdog in perpetuity; treat competitive overconfidence as a warning sign and actively correct the mental model when it arises.

After posting content, review your top 10 and bottom 10 pieces from the last month. Pick one specific thing the top 10 do that the bottom 10 do not, and implement it in every piece going forward. Accumulate this into a personal checklist.

When setting phone appointments from inbound leads, lead with your name and pause ('John?' then 'This is Alex'), add humor and self-deprecating energy, and close by asking what time works rather than whether they want to come in.
Whenever you feel impatient that results are not arriving fast enough, use that feeling as a trigger to increase input actions rather than as a prompt to monitor outcomes more closely.
Accumulate failures in a new skill as fast as possible and without self-judgment; treat each failure as eliminating one wrong path rather than as evidence of incompetence.

When judging whether you are progressing fast enough, compare your current state to where you started — not to where others are now. Observers see the current state of successful people, not the years of detours they took.
topic: All Life Paths Have Equal Suffering; Outcome Differs by Choice

text: If you are failing at a high-complexity goal, diagnose whether you are missing prerequisite skills before concluding you lack natural ability. Take two steps back to build the foundation if necessary.
Treat failures as completed action steps that increase your probability of success, not as evidence that reduces it. Get the failures out of the way faster.

Calculate your true hourly rate by dividing annual income by 8,000 (approximate waking hours in a year) or by 2,000 (forty-hour workweek) and use that number as the threshold for evaluating whether an activity is worth your time.

For each activity you do in a month, estimate the total hours and total income generated, calculate the hourly return, and compare it to your personal average. Prioritize maximizing hours on activities that exceed the average; minimize or delegate activities that fall below.

If you have a proven active income source generating above-average returns, reinvest profits into multiplication (hiring, marketing, tooling) for that activity rather than investing into new passive income experiments.

When scaling a business, systematically diagnose which of the 8 business functions (product, marketing, sales, customer success, recruiting, IT, HR, finance) is the binding constraint at your revenue stage, then deploy standardized solutions from the $100 Million Scaling Roadmap.

Allocate significant founder time (2 days per week minimum) to recruiting and core team building when entering a new scaling phase, prioritizing leadership-layer hires that enable leverage over day-to-day execution.

Comment below this video stating what specific action you will take today—not a New Year's resolution, not a future commitment, but something concrete you will do within 24 hours if it is truly important enough to pursue.

Examine your bank account and calendar at the end of each month or quarter, and use these two inputs to determine your true priorities and identity. Compare stated goals to actual spending and time allocation to surface areas of misalignment.

When adopting a new identity, allocate money or calendar time immediately as a commitment device, not after you have been the new identity. The spending or scheduling change should precede the behavior shift.

Invest a portion of discretionary capital explicitly in skills, education, courses, and coaching rather than consumption. Track skill-investment spending separately from stuff-buying to maintain visibility on the wealth-building components of your spending.
Develop your personal excellence bar by setting incremental quality targets; measure progress as your standard rises over months and years.
Extend your time horizon beyond immediate results; practice committing to longer projects (weeks, months, years) to build delayed-gratification muscle.
Visit acquisition.com/roadmap to download the 10-stage business growth roadmap from zero to $100M+; enter your information to receive the free framework.
Use the 10-stage roadmap as a diagnostic tool: identify your current stage by headcount and function constraints, then reference the symptom list and graduation steps for your vertical.
Risk rejection now rather than guarantee regret later.
Handle the level of rejection in business the same way you handle job search rejection.
Focus on preparation and competitive advantage relative to others, not on the excitement of winning.
When uncertain about passion or direction, commit to becoming good at something by doing it repeatedly, even when performing poorly initially. Passion emerges from competence, not the reverse.

Evaluate early-career roles not primarily on salary, but on the quality of peers and the learning velocity offered. Prioritize proximity to excellence and global brand credibility over immediate income.
Ground career decisions in long-term goal clarity (10+ year horizon) rather than comparing yourself to social media outliers or the 0.0001% success rate.
Before selecting an ownership model (owner-operator vs. subcontractor/franchise), explicitly define your personal goal and your speed-to-scale target.
When scaling a remodeling or service business, understand the constraint symptoms and graduation criteria across the 10 stages of growth (available via acquisition.com/roadmap).
Evaluate each business model not as objectively better/worse, but as a choice between different categories of problems you will solve and problems you will accept.

Run a time study once per year: record your activity in 15-minute blocks for one full week. Note one word per block describing what you did. This single week becomes your most productive week because it forces visibility into task allocation.

Document all recurring decisions as if-then rules. When a customer contacts you with a request, if it is a duplicate request type, you should have a clear protocol that team members can execute without escalation.

Set approval thresholds by dollar amount and role. Below $500: no approval required. $500-$1,000: ops staff approves. Above $1,000: founder approves. Use monthly caps to constrain total discretionary authority per person.

Prioritize task delegation in three phases: green tasks first (quick delegation to existing staff), yellow tasks second (one-time process builds), red tasks last (new hires or skill development). This sequence maximizes early wins.
Do not use Lamborghini or Rolex imagery to appeal to high-wealth audiences; use demonstrated customer results instead.
Build creator credibility through delivered customer outcomes rather than through aspirational lifestyle signaling.

Find ways to win in the meantime while pursuing a larger uncertain goal; these interim wins bridge the emotional gap between the motivational narrative (30-second montage) and the lived reality (5+ years of grinding).

When facing repeated status losses or doubts, identify and consciously accept the worst-case scenario (e.g., returning home a failure) as the true cost, and then ask whether continuing is psychologically cheaper than that outcome.

Build a repeatable fallback plan (e.g., Uber + secondary income + lower living cost) that allows you to restart your primary venture multiple times without hitting a hard floor, so commitment to the venture is decoupled from outcome certainty.
When evaluating content performance, prioritize direct feedback from target avatar (IRL responses, direct messages from business owners, etc.) over vanity metrics like view count.

Calculate the addressable market size for your avatar (using publicly available census data on business ownership, income, geography, etc.) and set view-count expectations based on penetration of that market, not on mass-entertainment benchmarks.
When designing content for a niche avatar, expect view counts to be significantly lower than mass-appeal content, and interpret this as a feature (audience quality), not a bug (low reach).
Produce more of the content format that your in-person / highest-trust audience members explicitly prefer, even if it generates lower view counts than other content types.

Place your business information into the $100 million scaling roadmap quiz at acquisition.com/roadmap to identify your growth stage and the critical function (product, marketing, sales, customer success, recruiting, IT, HR, finance) to optimize next.
Book a call with Hormozi's team via the roadmap tool's thank-you page to have your business evaluated; if they can help scale it, they will invite you to an in-person workshop in Vegas.
For service businesses without capital to scale mass-market, position upmarket and target customers with existing wealth rather than attempting to serve price-sensitive segments.

Set customer expectations to zero and deliver pleasant surprises rather than promising the world and failing to fulfill, particularly in premium service positioning where customer expectations are already inflated.

Specialize in either scalable information/software products targeting mass market OR premium service positioning targeting upmarket; combining both segments on a single brand creates operational and reputational damage.
When facing a high-pressure decision with a disapproving family member, create physical distance before announcing the decision, to prevent real-time counter-persuasion.

Attend marketing workshops and educational events relevant to your industry, even if they seem tangential to your immediate plan, because accidental discoveries (like Facebook ads for a gym owner) can become strategic pivots.
Frame small behavioral wins in negative emotions or adversity as incremental progress ('one W at a time, just one W at a time') rather than requiring large changes.
Start decision-making by working backward from end-of-life values: ask what you want to be remembered for, then align present behavior to those values.

When you recognize you are in a bad mood or have experienced adverse circumstances, consciously maintain respect, love, appreciation, and gratitude toward others; treat that one interaction or one day with full presence as a personal win regardless of internal state.
Separate the question of fairness from the question of agency: excuses may be legitimate, but they do not change your obligation to solve the problem or accept the consequence of inaction.

Use the roadmap framework to map your current business stage, identify the eight functions, and confirm the specific constraint symptoms; then execute the documented graduation steps for your stage rather than inventing a custom path.
When facing resistance to action, replace the question 'Can I do this?' with 'What is required?' and commit to executing the required action regardless of confidence level.
Build decision-making on the assumption that the cost is conscious: every time you make a choice, you are making an explicit trade. Own that trade instead of disguising it as circumstance.

When consuming information or attending educational events, filter every piece against one criterion: will this change my behavior in the conditions I face? If the answer is no, either reject the information or recognize that you are not receiving it. Apply this test ruthlessly to cut through filler.

When a person states an objection in a sales context, affirm their objection directly ('you're right, you'll never succeed') and observe whether they defend against that agreement or accept it. If they defend, the objection is not their true belief; if they accept, it may be structural and require a different approach.

Reframe stated excuses by validating them as the precise reason to act: 'I don't have time' becomes 'that's the perfect reason you should do it'; 'I don't have money' becomes 'that's the perfect reason you should do it.' Use direct reframe rather than debate or cajolery.

Build your decision-making and persuasion filters around observable behavior, not thought, mood, or identity. Ignore psychological frameworks (manifesting, affirmations, identity work) if they do not lead to behavior change; focus on the activities that directly produce measurable outcomes.

During the exploitation phase, explicitly choose to isolate from networking events and collaboration asks in favor of focused execution; treat this as a seasonal choice, not a permanent social withdrawal.
Regularly audit your inner circle and shed relationships that are low-alignment with your current objectives; frame this as a season ending, not a personal rejection of those individuals.

When seeking advice on major decisions, consult only people whose actual outcomes (not intentions) you admire; explicitly avoid seeking input from peers in your current reference group if they have not achieved your target outcomes.

Practice saying no to exploratory opportunities, collaboration asks, and networking events as a skill; treat it as deliberately uncomfortable and necessary to the transition from exploration to exploitation.

Build your close circle with people who are one level above your current status and with whom you have work-ethic alignment; initiate these relationships by demonstrating execution, not by asking for help upfront.

When confronted with a self-narrative like 'I have demons' or 'I self-sabotage,' translate it into observable behavioral terms first (Logic), then audit how many times that behavior has actually occurred (Evidence), then ask whether it actually matters relative to your goals (Utility) before deciding whether to act on it.

If you are going through hardship, reframe it as the origin chapter of the person you want to become. Ask: if I wanted to design the ideal version of myself as a competitor and achiever, what would I need to go through? Then recognize that the current difficulty is likely that thing.

Stop spending time explaining or narrating things that you can simply move on from. Most past events can be left behind by changing the behavior they created aversively — identify the condition, identify the current behavior, decide whether that behavior is conducive to your goals, then stack the deck to shift the response.

When identifying peak performance behaviors in sales (or any skill domain), isolate the specific observable differences between your best and worst states — pause length, question timing, tonality — and practice those behaviors explicitly so they become reproducible rather than state-dependent.
Do not search for shortcuts; accept that they do not lead to desired destinations and recognize the time wasted searching exceeds the time required for the hard way.
Prepare for the never-ending onslaught of difficulty; maintain awareness that you signed up for this difficulty and that enduring it is the only choice available.
Use the 10-stage roadmap (available at acquisition.com/roadmap) to understand the predictable constraints at each scaling stage and the eight business functions that require attention.

When faced with a limiting belief or a pattern of failure, reframe the external circumstance as the other person's or group's challenge, and recognize their success within those constraints. Then apply the same reframe to yourself.

Before studying books, tactics, or frameworks to improve a capability, first explicitly state and accept: 'My fault. My responsibility. All me. I am source.' This is the precondition for all other learning.

When approaching a relationship repair or conflict, lead with accountability and understanding rather than defensiveness. Say what you understand about the other person's position, not what you disagree with.
When hiring, explicitly identify whether a candidate is joining for growth or to contribute their expertise; avoid hiring those seeking advancement/titles in middle-career phases.
Structure senior-talent compensation and roles to reward meaningful impact and mastery, not advancement or titles, so they remain intrinsically motivated.
Decompose customer success goals (product love, referrals) into granular metrics and tactics: messaging timing, friction reduction, incentive design.
Block time specifically to work on the business (strategy, hiring, systems) rather than just working in the business (daily operations, production, delivery).
Hire your first employees and delegate production and revenue-generating tasks to decouple the business from sole founder capacity.
Adopt a 30,000-foot strategic perspective to identify and plan around obstacles rather than repeatedly encountering them tactically.

When pitching a premium offer (e.g., on-time on-budget guarantee), lead with the typical failure case (10-20% overrun, 3-9 month delay) so the homeowner anchors to that loss before hearing the price premium. This anchoring reframes the premium fee as small relative to the avoided loss.

Pair a risk-reduction guarantee with an explicit constraint that prevents the guarantee from being exploited (e.g., 'no scope changes'). Explain the constraint clearly and positively so the homeowner understands it as a prerequisite, not a punishment.

Specialize in value optimization (ensuring the home will appraise high) so that you can justify premium pricing without being seen as simply charging more. The higher appraisal is the evidence for the premium fee.

Become a deeper A-player in your core domain if you want to attract and retain A-player talent. Reading, training, and practicing your craft are non-negotiable prerequisites to building an elite team.

Evaluate hiring decisions using capital-allocation ROI logic: compare the annual profit generated by a role to the fully-loaded acquisition cost (salary + benefits + recruiting fees + onboarding). If annual profit is $700k, a $150k investment is justified.

When growth is stalled, audit founder depth and credibility in your business's core function before blaming market conditions or talent availability. The founder is almost always the binding constraint.
In the age of AI, prioritize recruiting high-leverage talent (engineers, operators, specialists) ahead of hiring breadth, since individual leverage is multiplied by AI tooling.

Block the first hour of every Monday on your calendar, labeled Solomon. Use it to conduct a written dialogue simulating conversation with your 85-year-old future self. Write as yourself, then respond as your future self, iterating until you reach a genuine resolution rather than a rationalized one.

When naming a social fear (what will people think), force yourself to name the actual individuals whose opinion you are deferring to, then evaluate whether each specific person's opinion genuinely warrants the behavioral constraint you are imposing on yourself.

As a variation on conventional gratitude journaling, imagine yourself as your 85-year-old future self who has been reborn into your present-day life. Walk through ordinary morning experiences (waking next to your partner, looking out the window, noticing physical pain is absent) from that aged perspective to restore appreciation that hedonic adaptation has eroded.

Continue a Solomon session until you reach a resolution that you cannot talk yourself out of, not just a comfortable stopping point. If a part of you suspects you are still enrolled in your own story, keep pushing.

If you are a business owner not growing as fast as desired, use the $100 million scaling roadmap quiz (acquisition.com/roadmap) to identify your current growth stage and the most critical function to optimize (product, marketing, sales, customer success, recruiting, IT, HR, finance).

Implement AI automation by customizing it to your specific delivery workflows and sales process rather than deploying out-of-box solutions. Out-of-box AI tools will not deliver viable results; success requires integration and tuning to your domain.

When a tactic fails, break it into component parts and ask 'what about this didn't work?' instead of 'did this work or not?' This granular questioning reveals which specific lever (ad hook, offer clarity, page congruence, problem fit) is the actual constraint.

If a business has a viable foundational principle (solves a real problem, profitable unit economics), always diagnose by asking 'what is the constraint holding us back?' rather than questioning whether the business model itself is viable.

When iterating through failures, separate the outcome (business result) from identity (self-worth). Develop tolerance for repeated failures as a necessary part of building expertise, not as evidence of personal inadequacy.

Translate vague outcomes (user engagement, conversion, growth) into micro-metrics (10 friends in 14 days, click-through rate, average order value) that are testable and directly actionable by the product or marketing team.
Document your life during struggle, not during success. Capture the moments you want to look away from: sleeping on floors, losing sales, financial scarcity, equipment failure.
When facing a relational or emotional problem that feels unsolvable, try the frame 'that's okay' to accept it as a fact rather than as a problem requiring solution.
Reframe current struggle as the backstory your future self will use to stand confidently before others; treat hardship as narrative evidence rather than as a mistake.
Measure your focus by the quantity and quality of things you say no to.
Burn your boats: eliminate all alternatives by structuring your life such that pursuing other opportunities becomes difficult.
When encountering a peer's success in a new domain, explicitly acknowledge the invisible costs and problems, then consciously reaffirm commitment to your current focus.
Define commitment operationally as the elimination of alternatives, not as enthusiasm or optimism.

When learning a new skill through activity, measure and isolate the top 10% of your outputs (sales calls, content pieces, outreach attempts, customer success interactions) and explicitly analyze what made them different from the baseline 90%.

After identifying differentiating factors from your top 10%, deliberately frontload those factors into your next cycle of high-volume activity and intentionally try new variables in the remaining space to capture additional refinements.

Maintain a visible checklist or system documenting the factors and optimizations you extract from each volume cycle; treat the checklist as a living artifact that evolves as you discover new micro-improvements.

Accept ownership of everything that has passed to this moment—all the missed gym days, all the skipped diets, all the unsaved money. Do not cast blame to family, circumstance, country of birth, or zip code.
When facing systemic or personal obstacles, choose being rich over being right about why you are not rich; defending a narrative of external cause forecloses the actions required to change.
Master foundational behaviors first—showing up on time, keeping commitments, basic consistency—before pursuing advanced tactics. Do not skip to calculus; ensure addition is solid.

Save money one dollar at a time over years (e.g., five years for the first $100k), accepting that early capital accumulation is entirely behavioral and cannot be rushed or arbitraged away without prior wins.

Diagnose founder motivation barriers using the 10x money test: ask 'If this business made 10 times the money, would you keep doing it?' If yes, fix the business economics. If no, the problem is purpose misalignment, not revenue insufficiency.

Identify an external purpose—something outside yourself that the business serves as a vehicle toward (personal identity development, societal problem-solving, impact creation)—and use it as the primary motivational anchor for the business.

Restructure the business to support the founder's external purpose and personal fulfillment, even if the restructuring reduces short-term profitability or efficiency, because founder sustainability is a more binding constraint than business optimization.

Keep the external purpose and founder motivation continuously front-of-mind as the primary strategic variable guiding business decisions, because the founder's willingness to persist is the greatest constraint on business continuity.
Stack as many advantages as you can: sleep on time, do not drink, get in shape, do repetitions, humble yourself with people more experienced than you.
If pursuing ambitious goals, argue the opposite case—that drinking more will help—and notice that you cannot make it; therefore abstain.
Choose your reference group deliberately; sometimes you have to like your goals more than you like your friends.
Go to acquisition.com/roadmap, plug in business information, get personalized scaling diagnostics, and book a call with the team if you want in-person analysis.

When diagnosing organizational underperformance, start by examining the leader of the underperforming function rather than jumping to tactical solutions (pricing changes, sales process redesigns, product improvements).
topic: Leadership Sets Culture; Culture Determines Acceptable Effort

text: If a leader is underperforming, remove them immediately rather than attempting to fix them. The cost of a broken leader is always greater than the cost of management change.
topic: Leadership Sets Culture; Culture Determines Acceptable Effort

text: Spend almost exclusively on information and knowledge access, treating every other discretionary category as secondary. Evaluate any knowledge purchase by asking whether buying someone else's 10 years of experience compresses your learning enough to justify the fee at your current opportunity cost.

Maintain a large cash reserve that preserves offensive optionality rather than fully deploying capital into passive index vehicles; accept the foregone passive return in exchange for the ability to move quickly on large, asymmetric opportunities.

If a truly passive investment strategy is the goal, invest in a dividend ETF (3-4% yield) and treat dividend growth as the game metric; structure to take advantage of qualified dividend capital gains tax rates (~20-23%) rather than ordinary income tax treatment.

When evaluating whether to take a feared action, mentally extend the scenario two or three moves beyond the feared bad event to expose the post-disruption equilibrium, which is typically better than the current mediocre state.

To build a different version of yourself, begin accruing small pieces of behavioral evidence that are consistent with the target identity rather than waiting until the identity is formed before acting.
Before adopting any belief, test whether you can explain the reasoning behind it in your own words; if you cannot, treat it as borrowed rather than your own.
Adopt an infinite-game frame: define winning as continued participation in the game, not achievement of any finite metric, so that defeat becomes logically impossible as long as you keep playing.
When you have clear 10-year wealth target and mental commitment, act as if you will absolutely achieve that outcome; make compounding bets and abandon short-term income obsession.
In early career when time is abundant and capital is scarce, prioritize skill investment and experience accumulation (SME 500) over financial asset diversification (S&P 500).

Shift decision-making framework from 'how much money can I make this year' to 'what would I have to do to make it unreasonable that I don't 10x in 10 years', then execute against that long-term constraint.

Adopt a seasonal framing for multi-year business phases: roughly 3 years of focused execution, followed by 2 years of transition or reflection. This provides natural closure boundaries and reduces decision heaviness.

Document and share the best practices, failures, and lessons from your businesses through books, content, or teaching; treat the business as a vehicle for knowledge transfer rather than purely as profit generation.

Stop judging yourself for your work preferences; establish a schedule that reflects your genuine motivation (e.g., 5 AM - 4 PM with gym break) and reject external definitions of balance that do not align with your values.
Take purposeful action despite fear or discomfort in order to gain knowledge, because confidence is a retroactive result of action, not a precondition.
