Before accepting any new initiative or change, require the expected upside to be greater than 20% on the relevant metric, since any change incurs a ~20% guaranteed downside during transition.
If a business function's metrics are at or above industry benchmark, explicitly decide to leave it alone and redirect the time and attention it was receiving to the actual binding constraint.

When running recurring events or structured programs, establish a rule of zero new changes for multiple cycles and measure NPS or equivalent satisfaction metrics; only introduce changes after baseline performance is fully documented.
topic: Execution and Rapid Adjustment Over Planning

text: Apply Warren Buffett's punch-card discipline to strategic decisions: imagine you have one punch per year for a business improvement; use this constraint to force identification of the genuinely highest-leverage action rather than the most interesting or comfortable one.
Managers should ask makers directly: what does a maximally productive day look like for you? Then adjust meeting scheduling to accommodate that ideal as closely as possible.

Makers should batch meetings into designated windows (e.g., Monday and Thursday afternoons) and direct all meeting requests to those windows rather than accepting ad hoc interruptions throughout the week.

When a meeting is forced into a maker's morning, the maker should convert the entire disrupted day into a manager day by stacking as many other pending meetings as possible into the already-contaminated block rather than leaving the rest of the day as fragmented maker time.

At the end of every recurring meeting, ask two questions: Do I need to do this again? Can a process or another person replace my presence here? If yes to either, remove yourself or eliminate the meeting.

Communicate to all collaborators which hours you will be slow to respond (maker blocks) and which hours you will be fully responsive (manager blocks), and then actually be responsive during the promised windows to maintain credibility.

Operators should adopt a shared vocabulary (maker mode, manager mode, maker's no, maker days) and communicate which mode they are operating in for any given day so that team members can calibrate their expectations and approach appropriately.

Organizations should consider mandated quiet time — either specific hours each day or full quiet days per week — where maker-role employees cannot be messaged or pulled into meetings, enabling sustained deep work across the team simultaneously.

When raising prices on existing customers, send a teaser email first (big news coming tomorrow), then in the main email: remind them of value delivered, announce the increase, explain reinvestment rationale and what they receive in return, note that new customers are already paying the higher price, and offer a loyalty discount equal to the current price for the next three to six months before the new price kicks in. Include a PS inviting those for whom the increase is a genuine hardship to reach out individually.

To identify and force an activation point: look at all retained customers and identify what behaviors they performed early that non-retained customers did not. Systematize onboarding to drive all new customers to that specific early behavior.

To identify product features worth keeping: write out every feature your service provides, then survey customers with the question 'If I got rid of everything except one thing, which would you want to keep?' Remove the lowest-ranked feature without announcement and observe who complains. If no one complains, retire the feature permanently.

Track both qualified ascension rate (of customers who were eligible to ascend, what percentage did?) and total ascension rate (of all customers, what percentage ascended?) together; qualified rate measures conversion quality, total rate measures how well the business surfaces eligible customers.

When context notes on every customer conversation are maintained and shared across all customer-facing reps, never require a customer to repeat their history or goals to a new rep — rephrasing the customer's own stated goal back to them at each interaction is the minimum standard for high-retention CS operations.

Before opening a second business location, the founder must be able to leave for two to four weeks with their phone off and return to find the business maintained or grown. Passing this test is the prerequisite for expansion.

When hiring CS or delivery staff after a turnaround, bring in new higher-compensated talent alongside the existing team (the dilution method) rather than firing everyone at once. Better performers will naturally expose lower performers, many of whom will voluntarily exit once the culture shifts.
Keep a part-time job during the first phase of building a drop-servicing business until you generate at least one consistent daily client, then quit.
topic: All Life Paths Have Equal Suffering; Outcome Differs by Choice

text: When producing student testimonial videos for a coaching or course business, conduct unscripted interviews rather than pre-written Q&A to preserve authenticity signals for a skeptical audience.
When a verification step fails in a business setup (e.g., Google Business Profile verification), treat it as a process discovery problem rather than evidence the model does not work.

When starting a remote service arbitrage (GMB) business, immediately create as many Google My Business profiles as possible, then focus all energy on acquiring legitimate reviews for each profile before doing anything else.
Monitor your call provider log daily when using a VA for call answering; non-performance is visible on day one through missed call counts.
Screen VAs for call-answering roles for accent compatibility with the target market during the initial day of hiring evaluation.
